science of spiritual knowledge, gave up his body. Vasiñöha, the
great-grandfather, gave up his body also, but through the semen
discharged by Mitra and Varuëa when they saw Urvaçé, he was born
again.

text: During the performance of the yajïa, the body relinquished
sanskrit:
by Mahäräja Nimi was preserved in fragrant substances, and at the end
of the Satra-yäga the great saints and brähmaëas made the following
request to all the demigods assembled there.

text: "If you are satisfied with this sacrifice and if you are
sanskrit:
actually able to do so, kindly bring Mahäräja Nimi back to life in
this body." The demigods said yes to this request by the sages, but
Mahäräja Nimi said, "Please do not imprison me again in a material
body."

text: Mahäräja Nimi continued: Mäyävädés generally want
sanskrit:
freedom from accepting a material body because they fear having to give
it up again. But devotees whose intelligence is always filled with the
service of the Lord are unafraid. Indeed, they take advantage of the
body to render transcendental loving service.

text: I do not wish to accept a material body, for such a body is
sanskrit:
the source of all distress, lamentation and fear, everywhere in the
universe, just as it is for a fish in the water, which lives always in
anxiety because of fear of death.

text: The demigods said: Let Mahäräja Nimi live without a
sanskrit:
material body. Let him live in a spiritual body as a personal associate
of the Supreme Personality of Godhead, and, according to his desire, let
him be manifest or unmanifest to common materially embodied people.

text: Thereafter, to save the people from the danger of an
sanskrit:
unregulated government, the sages churned Mahäräja Nimi's material
body, from which, as a result, a son was born.

text: Because he was born in an unusual way, the son was called
sanskrit:
Janaka, and because he was born from the dead body of his father, he was
known as Vaideha. Because he was born from the churning of his father's
material body, he was known as Mithila, and because he constructed a
city as King Mithila, the city was called Mithilä.

text: O King Parékñit, from Mithila came a son named Udävasu;
sanskrit:
from Udävasu, Nandivardhana; from Nandivardhana, Suketu; and from
Suketu, Devaräta.

text: From Devaräta came a son named Båhadratha and from
sanskrit:
Båhadratha a son named Mahävérya, who became the father of Sudhåti.
The son of Sudhåti was known as Dhåñöaketu, and from Dhåñöaketu
came Haryaçva. From Haryaçva came a son named Maru.

text: The son of Maru was Pratépaka, and the son of Pratépaka
sanskrit:
was Kåtaratha. From Kåtaratha came Devaméòha; from Devaméòha,
Viçruta; and from Viçruta, Mahädhåti.

text: From Mahädhåti was born a son named Kåtiräta, from
sanskrit:
Kåtiräta was born Mahäromä, from Mahäromä came a son named
Svarëaromä, and from Svarëaromä came Hrasvaromä.

text: From Hrasvaromä came a son named Çéradhvaja [also called
sanskrit:
Janaka]. When Çéradhvaja was plowing a field, from the front of his
plow [çéra] appeared a daughter named Sétädevé, who later became
the wife of Lord Rämacandra. Thus he was known as Çéradhvaja.

text: The son of Çéradhvaja was Kuçadhvaja, and the son of
sanskrit:
Kuçadhvaja was King Dharmadhvaja, who had two sons, namely Kåtadhvaja
and Mitadhvaja.

text: O Mahäräja Parékñit, the son of Kåtadhvaja was
sanskrit:
Keçidhvaja, and the son of Mitadhvaja was Khäëòikya. The son of
Kåtadhvaja was expert in spiritual knowledge, and the son of Mitadhvaja
was expert in Vedic ritualistic ceremonies. Khäëòikya fled in fear of
Keçidhvaja. The son of Keçidhvaja was Bhänumän, and the son of
Bhänumän was Çatadyumna.

text: The son of Çatadyumna was named Çuci. From Çuci,
sanskrit:
Sanadväja was born, and from Sanadväja came a son named Ürjaketu. The
son of Ürjaketu was Aja, and the son of Aja was Purujit.

text: The son of Purujit was Ariñöanemi, and his son was
sanskrit:
Çrutäyu. Çrutäyu begot a son named Supärçvaka, and Supärçvaka
begot Citraratha. The son of Citraratha was Kñemädhi, who became the
king of Mithilä.

text: The son of Kñemädhi was Samaratha, and his son was
sanskrit:
Satyaratha. The son of Satyaratha was Upaguru, and the son of Upaguru
was Upagupta, a partial expansion of the fire-god.

text: The son of Upagupta was Vasvananta, the son of Vasvananta
sanskrit:
was Yuyudha, the son of Yuyudha was Subhäñaëa, and the son of
Subhäñaëa was Çruta. The son of Çruta was Jaya, from whom there
came Vijaya. The son of Vijaya was Åta.

text: The son of Åta was Çunaka, the son of Çunaka was
sanskrit:
Vétahavya, the son of Vétahavya was Dhåti, and the son of Dhåti was
Bahuläçva. The son of Bahuläçva was Kåti, and his son was
Mahävaçé.

text: Çukadeva Gosvämé said: My dear King Parékñit, all the
sanskrit:
kings of the dynasty of Mithila were completely in knowledge of their
spiritual identity. Therefore, even though staying at home, they were
liberated from the duality of material existence.

text: Çréla Çukadeva Gosvämé said to Mahäräja Parékñit: O
sanskrit:
King, thus far you have heard the description of the dynasty of the
sun-god. Now hear the most glorious and purifying description of the
dynasty of the moon-god. This description mentions kings like Aila
[Purüravä] of whom it is glorious to hear.

text: Lord Viñëu [Garbhodakaçäyé Viñëu] is also known as
sanskrit:
Sahasra-çérñä Puruña. From the lake of His navel sprang a lotus, on
which Lord Brahmä was generated. Atri, the son of Lord Brahmä, was as
qualified as his father.

text: From Atri's tears of jubilation was born a son named Soma,
sanskrit:
the moon, who was full of soothing rays. Lord Brahmä appointed him the
director of the brähmaëas, drugs and luminaries.

text: After conquering the three worlds [the upper, middle and
sanskrit:
lower planetary systems], Soma, the moon-god, performed a great
sacrifice known as the Räjasüya-yajïa. Because he was very much
puffed up, he forcibly kidnapped Båhaspati's wife, whose name was
Tärä.

text: Although requested again and again by Båhaspati, the
sanskrit:
spiritual master of the demigods, Soma did not return Tärä. This was
due to his false pride. Consequently, a fight ensued between the
demigods and the demons.

text: Because of enmity between Båhaspati and Çukra, Çukra took
sanskrit:
the side of the moon-god and was joined by the demons. But Lord Çiva,
because of affection for the son of his spiritual master, joined the
side of Båhaspati and was accompanied by all the ghosts and hobgoblins.

text: King Indra, accompanied by all kinds of demigods, joined the
sanskrit:
side of Båhaspati. Thus there was a great fight, destroying both demons
and demigods, only for the sake of Tärä, Båhaspati's wife.

text: When Lord Brahmä was fully informed by Aìgirä about the
sanskrit:
entire incident, he severely chastised the moon-god, Soma. Thus Lord
Brahmä delivered Tärä to her husband, who could then understand that
she was pregnant.

text: Båhaspati said: You foolish woman, your womb, which was
sanskrit:
meant for me to impregnate, has been impregnated by someone other than
me. Immediately deliver your child! Immediately deliver it! Be assured
that after the child is delivered, I shall not burn you to ashes. I know
that although you are unchaste, you wanted a son. Therefore I shall not
punish you.

text: Çukadeva Gosvämé continued: By Båhaspati's order,
sanskrit:
Tärä, who was very much ashamed, immediately gave birth to the child,
who was very beautiful, with a golden bodily hue. Both Båhaspati and
the moon-god, Soma, desired the beautiful child.

text: Fighting again broke out between Båhaspati and the
sanskrit:
moon-god, both of whom claimed, "This is my child, not yours!" All the
saints and demigods present asked Tärä whose child the newborn baby
actually was, but because she was ashamed she could not immediately
answer.

text: The child then became very angry and demanded that his
sanskrit:
mother immediately tell the truth. "You unchaste woman," he said, "what
is the use of your unnecessary shame? Why do you not admit your fault?
Immediately tell me about your faulty behavior."

text: Lord Brahmä then brought Tärä to a secluded place, and
sanskrit:
after pacifying her he asked to whom the child actually belonged. She
replied very slowly, "This is the son of Soma, the moon-god." Then the
moon-god immediately took charge of the child.

text: O Mahäräja Parékñit, when Lord Brahmä saw that the
sanskrit:
child was deeply intelligent, he gave the child the name Budha. The
moon-god, the ruler of the stars, enjoyed great jubilation because of
this son.

text: Thereafter, from Budha, through the womb of Ilä, a son
sanskrit:
was born named Purüravä, who was described in the beginning of the
Ninth Canto. When his beauty, personal qualities, magnanimity, behavior,
wealth and power were described by Närada in the court of Lord Indra,
the celestial woman Urvaçé was attracted to him. Pierced by the arrow
of Cupid, she thus approached him.

text: Having been cursed by Mitra and Varuëa, the celestial
sanskrit:
woman Urvaçé had acquired the habits of a human being. Therefore, upon
seeing Purüravä, the best of males, whose beauty resembled that of
Cupid, she controlled herself and then approached him. When King
Purüravä saw Urvaçé, his eyes became jubilant in the ecstasy of joy,
and the hairs on his body stood on end. With mild, pleasing words, he
spoke to her as follows.

text: King Purüravä said: O most beautiful woman, you are
sanskrit:
welcome. Please sit here and tell me what I can do for you. You may
enjoy with me as long as you desire. Let us pass our life happily in a
sexual relationship.

text: Urvaçé replied: O most handsome man, who is the woman
sanskrit:
whose mind and sight would not be attracted by you? If a woman takes
shelter of your chest, she cannot refuse to enjoy with you in a sexual
relationship.

text: My dear King Purüravä, please give protection to these
sanskrit:
two lambs, who have fallen down with me. Although I belong to the
heavenly planets and you belong to earth, I shall certainly enjoy sexual
union with you. I have no objection to accepting you as my husband, for
you are superior in every respect.

text: Urvaçé said: "My dear hero, only preparations made in
sanskrit:
ghee [clarified butter] will be my eatables, and I shall not want to see
you naked at any time, except at the time of sexual intercourse." The
great-minded King Purüravä accepted these proposals.

text: Purüravä replied: O beautiful one, your beauty is
sanskrit:
wonderful and your gestures are also wonderful. Indeed, you are
attractive to all human society. Therefore, since you have come of your
own accord from the heavenly planets, who on earth would not agree to
serve a demigoddess such as you.

text: Çukadeva Gosvämé continued: The best of human beings,
sanskrit:
Purüravä, began freely enjoying the company of Urvaçé, who engaged
in sexual activities with him in many celestial places, such as
Caitraratha and Nandana-känana, where the demigods enjoy.

text: Urvaçé's body was as fragrant as the saffron of a lotus.
sanskrit:
Being enlivened by the fragrance of her face and body, Purüravä
enjoyed her company for many days with great jubilation.

text: Not seeing Urvaçé in his assembly, the King of heaven,
sanskrit:
Lord Indra, said, "Without Urvaçé my assembly is no longer beautiful."
Considering this, he requested the Gandharvas to bring her back to his
heavenly planet.

text: Thus the Gandharvas came to earth, and at midnight, when
sanskrit:
everything was dark, they appeared in the house of Purüravä and stole
the two lambs entrusted to the King by his wife, Urvaçé.

text: Urvaçé treated the two lambs like her own sons.
sanskrit:
Therefore, when they were being taken by the Gandharvas and began
crying, Urvaçé heard them and rebuked her husband. "Now I am being
killed," she said, "under the protection of an unworthy husband, who is
a coward and a eunuch although he thinks himself a great hero.

text: "Because I depended on him, the plunderers have deprived me
sanskrit:
of my two sons the lambs, and therefore I am now lost. My husband lies
down at night in fear, exactly like a woman, although he appears to be a
man during the day."

text: Purüravä, stricken by the sharp words of Urvaçé like an
sanskrit:
elephant struck by its driver's pointed rod, became very angry. Not even
dressing himself properly, he took a sword in hand and went out naked
into the night to follow the Gandharvas who had stolen the lambs.

text: After giving up the two lambs, the Gandharvas shone
sanskrit:
brightly like lightning, thus illuminating the house of Purüravä.
Urvaçé then saw her husband returning with the lambs in hand, but he
was naked, and therefore she left.

text: No longer seeing Urvaçé on his bed, Purüravä was most
sanskrit:
aggrieved. Because of his great attraction for her, he was very much
disturbed. Thus, lamenting, he began traveling about the earth like a
madman.

text: Once during his travels all over the world, Purüravä saw
sanskrit:
Urvaçé, accompanied by five companions, on the bank of the Sarasvaté
at Kurukñetra. With jubilation in his face, he then spoke to her in
sweet words as follows.

text: O my dear wife, O most cruel one, kindly stay, kindly stay.
sanskrit:
I know that I have never made you happy until now, but you should not
give me up for that reason. This is not proper for you. Even if you have
decided to give up my company, let us nonetheless talk for some time.

text: O goddess, now that you have refused me, my beautiful body
sanskrit:
will fall down here, and because it is unsuitable for your pleasure, it
will be eaten by foxes and vultures.

text: Urvaçé said: My dear King, you are a man, a hero. Don't
sanskrit:
be impatient and give up your life. Be sober and don't allow the senses
to overcome you like foxes. Don't let the foxes eat you. In other words,
you should not be controlled by your senses. Rather, you should know
that the heart of a woman is like that of a fox. There is no use making
friendship with women.

text: Women as a class are merciless and cunning. They cannot
sanskrit:
tolerate even a slight offense. For their own pleasure they can do
anything irreligious, and therefore they do not fear killing even a
faithful husband or brother.

text: Women are very easily seduced by men. Therefore, polluted
sanskrit:
women give up the friendship of a man who is their well-wisher and
establish false friendship among fools. Indeed, they seek newer and
newer friends, one after another.

text: O my dear King, you will be able to enjoy with me as my
sanskrit:
husband at the end of every year, for one night only. In this way you
will have other children, one after another.

text: Understanding that Urvaçé was pregnant, Purüravä
sanskrit:
returned to his palace. At the end of the year, there at Kurukñetra, he
again obtained the association of Urvaçé, who was then the mother of a
heroic son.

text: Having regained Urvaçé at the end of the year, King
sanskrit:
Purüravä was most jubilant, and he enjoyed her company in sex for one
night. But then he was very sorry at the thought of separation from her,
so Urvaçé spoke to him as follows.

text: Urvaçé said: "My dear King, seek shelter of the
sanskrit:
Gandharvas, for they will be able to deliver me to you again." In
accordance with these words, the King satisfied the Gandharvas by
prayers, and the Gandharvas, being pleased with him, gave him an
Agnisthälé girl who looked exactly like Urvaçé. Thinking that the
girl was Urvaçé, the King began walking with her in the forest, but
later he could understand that she was not Urvaçé but Agnisthälé.

text: King Purüravä then left Agnisthälé in the forest and
sanskrit:
returned home, where he meditated all night upon Urvaçé. In the course
of his meditation, the Tretä millennium began, and therefore the
principles of the three Vedas, including the process of performing
yajïa to fulfill fruitive activities, appeared within his heart.

text: When the process of fruitive yajïa became manifest
sanskrit:
within his heart, King Purüravä went to the same spot where he had
left Agnisthälé. There he saw that from the womb of a çamé tree, an
açvattha tree had grown. He then took a piece of wood from that tree
and made it into two araëis. Desiring to go to the planet where
Urvaçé resided, he chanted mantras, meditating upon the lower araëi
as Urvaçé, the upper one as himself, and the piece of wood between
them as his son. In this way he began to ignite a fire.

text: From Purüravä's rubbing of the araëis came a fire. By
sanskrit:
such a fire one can achieve all success in material enjoyment and be
purified in seminal birth, initiation and in the performance of
sacrifice, which are invoked with the combined letters a-u-m. Thus the
fire was considered the son of King Purüravä.

text: By means of that fire, Purüravä, who desired to go to the
sanskrit:
planet where Urvaçé resided, performed a sacrifice, by which he
satisfied the Supreme Personality of Godhead, Hari, the enjoyer of the
results of sacrifice. Thus he worshiped the Lord, who is beyond the
perception of the senses and is the reservoir of all the demigods.

text: In the Satya-yuga, the first millennium, all the Vedic
sanskrit:
mantras were included in one mantra-praëava, the root of all Vedic
mantras. In other words, the Atharva Veda alone was the source of all
Vedic knowledge. The Supreme Personality of Godhead Näräyaëa was the
only worshipable Deity; there was no recommendation for worship of the
demigods. Fire was one only, and the only order of life in human society
was known as haàsa.

text: O Mahäräja Parékñit, at the beginning of Tretä-yuga,
sanskrit:
King Purüravä inaugurated a karma-käëòa sacrifice. Thus Purüravä,
who considered the yajïic fire his son, was able to go to Gandharvaloka
as he desired.

text: O my dear wife, O most cruel one, kindly stay, kindly stay.
sanskrit:
I know that I have never made you happy until now, but you should not
give me up for that reason. This is not proper for you. Even if you have
decided to give up my company, let us nonetheless talk for some time.

text: O goddess, now that you have refused me, my beautiful body
sanskrit:
will fall down here, and because it is unsuitable for your pleasure, it
will be eaten by foxes and vultures.

text: Urvaçé said: My dear King, you are a man, a hero. Don't
sanskrit:
be impatient and give up your life. Be sober and don't allow the senses
to overcome you like foxes. Don't let the foxes eat you. In other words,
you should not be controlled by your senses. Rather, you should know
that the heart of a woman is like that of a fox. There is no use making
friendship with women.

text: Women as a class are merciless and cunning. They cannot
sanskrit:
tolerate even a slight offense. For their own pleasure they can do
anything irreligious, and therefore they do not fear killing even a
faithful husband or brother.

text: Women are very easily seduced by men. Therefore, polluted
sanskrit:
women give up the friendship of a man who is their well-wisher and
establish false friendship among fools. Indeed, they seek newer and
newer friends, one after another.

text: O my dear King, you will be able to enjoy with me as my
sanskrit:
husband at the end of every year, for one night only. In this way you
will have other children, one after another.

text: Understanding that Urvaçé was pregnant, Purüravä
sanskrit:
returned to his palace. At the end of the year, there at Kurukñetra, he
again obtained the association of Urvaçé, who was then the mother of a
heroic son.

text: Having regained Urvaçé at the end of the year, King
sanskrit:
Purüravä was most jubilant, and he enjoyed her company in sex for one
night. But then he was very sorry at the thought of separation from her,
so Urvaçé spoke to him as follows.

text: Urvaçé said: "My dear King, seek shelter of the
sanskrit:
Gandharvas, for they will be able to deliver me to you again." In
accordance with these words, the King satisfied the Gandharvas by
prayers, and the Gandharvas, being pleased with him, gave him an
Agnisthälé girl who looked exactly like Urvaçé. Thinking that the
girl was Urvaçé, the King began walking with her in the forest, but
later he could understand that she was not Urvaçé but Agnisthälé.

text: King Purüravä then left Agnisthälé in the forest and
sanskrit:
returned home, where he meditated all night upon Urvaçé. In the course
of his meditation, the Tretä millennium began, and therefore the
principles of the three Vedas, including the process of performing
yajïa to fulfill fruitive activities, appeared within his heart.

text: When the process of fruitive yajïa became manifest
sanskrit:
within his heart, King Purüravä went to the same spot where he had
left Agnisthälé. There he saw that from the womb of a çamé tree, an
açvattha tree had grown. He then took a piece of wood from that tree
and made it into two araëis. Desiring to go to the planet where
Urvaçé resided, he chanted mantras, meditating upon the lower araëi
as Urvaçé, the upper one as himself, and the piece of wood between
them as his son. In this way he began to ignite a fire.

text: From Purüravä's rubbing of the araëis came a fire. By
sanskrit:
such a fire one can achieve all success in material enjoyment and be
purified in seminal birth, initiation and in the performance of
sacrifice, which are invoked with the combined letters a-u-m. Thus the
fire was considered the son of King Purüravä.

text: By means of that fire, Purüravä, who desired to go to the
sanskrit:
planet where Urvaçé resided, performed a sacrifice, by which he
satisfied the Supreme Personality of Godhead, Hari, the enjoyer of the
results of sacrifice. Thus he worshiped the Lord, who is beyond the
perception of the senses and is the reservoir of all the demigods.

text: In the Satya-yuga, the first millennium, all the Vedic
sanskrit:
mantras were included in one mantra-praëava, the root of all Vedic
mantras. In other words, the Atharva Veda alone was the source of all
Vedic knowledge. The Supreme Personality of Godhead Näräyaëa was the
only worshipable Deity; there was no recommendation for worship of the
demigods. Fire was one only, and the only order of life in human society
was known as haàsa.

text: O Mahäräja Parékñit, at the beginning of Tretä-yuga,
sanskrit:
King Purüravä inaugurated a karma-käëòa sacrifice. Thus Purüravä,
who considered the yajïic fire his son, was able to go to Gandharvaloka
as he desired.

text: Çréla Çukadeva Gosvämé said to Mahäräja Parékñit: O
sanskrit:
King, thus far you have heard the description of the dynasty of the
sun-god. Now hear the most glorious and purifying description of the
dynasty of the moon-god. This description mentions kings like Aila
[Purüravä] of whom it is glorious to hear.

text: Lord Viñëu [Garbhodakaçäyé Viñëu] is also known as
sanskrit:
Sahasra-çérñä Puruña. From the lake of His navel sprang a lotus, on
which Lord Brahmä was generated. Atri, the son of Lord Brahmä, was as
qualified as his father.

text: From Atri's tears of jubilation was born a son named Soma,
sanskrit:
the moon, who was full of soothing rays. Lord Brahmä appointed him the
director of the brähmaëas, drugs and luminaries.

text: After conquering the three worlds [the upper, middle and
sanskrit:
lower planetary systems], Soma, the moon-god, performed a great
sacrifice known as the Räjasüya-yajïa. Because he was very much
puffed up, he forcibly kidnapped Båhaspati's wife, whose name was
Tärä.

text: Although requested again and again by Båhaspati, the
sanskrit:
spiritual master of the demigods, Soma did not return Tärä. This was
due to his false pride. Consequently, a fight ensued between the
demigods and the demons.

text: Because of enmity between Båhaspati and Çukra, Çukra took
sanskrit:
the side of the moon-god and was joined by the demons. But Lord Çiva,
because of affection for the son of his spiritual master, joined the
side of Båhaspati and was accompanied by all the ghosts and hobgoblins.

text: King Indra, accompanied by all kinds of demigods, joined the
sanskrit:
side of Båhaspati. Thus there was a great fight, destroying both demons
and demigods, only for the sake of Tärä, Båhaspati's wife.

text: When Lord Brahmä was fully informed by Aìgirä about the
sanskrit:
entire incident, he severely chastised the moon-god, Soma. Thus Lord
Brahmä delivered Tärä to her husband, who could then understand that
she was pregnant.

text: Båhaspati said: You foolish woman, your womb, which was
sanskrit:
meant for me to impregnate, has been impregnated by someone other than
me. Immediately deliver your child! Immediately deliver it! Be assured
that after the child is delivered, I shall not burn you to ashes. I know
that although you are unchaste, you wanted a son. Therefore I shall not
punish you.

text: Çukadeva Gosvämé continued: By Båhaspati's order,
sanskrit:
Tärä, who was very much ashamed, immediately gave birth to the child,
who was very beautiful, with a golden bodily hue. Both Båhaspati and
the moon-god, Soma, desired the beautiful child.

text: Fighting again broke out between Båhaspati and the
sanskrit:
moon-god, both of whom claimed, "This is my child, not yours!" All the
saints and demigods present asked Tärä whose child the newborn baby
actually was, but because she was ashamed she could not immediately
answer.

text: The child then became very angry and demanded that his
sanskrit:
mother immediately tell the truth. "You unchaste woman," he said, "what
is the use of your unnecessary shame? Why do you not admit your fault?
Immediately tell me about your faulty behavior."

text: Lord Brahmä then brought Tärä to a secluded place, and
sanskrit:
after pacifying her he asked to whom the child actually belonged. She
replied very slowly, "This is the son of Soma, the moon-god." Then the
moon-god immediately took charge of the child.

text: O Mahäräja Parékñit, when Lord Brahmä saw that the
sanskrit:
child was deeply intelligent, he gave the child the name Budha. The
moon-god, the ruler of the stars, enjoyed great jubilation because of
this son.

text: Thereafter, from Budha, through the womb of Ilä, a son
sanskrit:
was born named Purüravä, who was described in the beginning of the
Ninth Canto. When his beauty, personal qualities, magnanimity, behavior,
wealth and power were described by Närada in the court of Lord Indra,
the celestial woman Urvaçé was attracted to him. Pierced by the arrow
of Cupid, she thus approached him.

text: Having been cursed by Mitra and Varuëa, the celestial
sanskrit:
woman Urvaçé had acquired the habits of a human being. Therefore, upon
seeing Purüravä, the best of males, whose beauty resembled that of
Cupid, she controlled herself and then approached him. When King
Purüravä saw Urvaçé, his eyes became jubilant in the ecstasy of joy,
and the hairs on his body stood on end. With mild, pleasing words, he
spoke to her as follows.

text: King Purüravä said: O most beautiful woman, you are
sanskrit:
welcome. Please sit here and tell me what I can do for you. You may
enjoy with me as long as you desire. Let us pass our life happily in a
sexual relationship.

text: Urvaçé replied: O most handsome man, who is the woman
sanskrit:
whose mind and sight would not be attracted by you? If a woman takes
shelter of your chest, she cannot refuse to enjoy with you in a sexual
relationship.

text: My dear King Purüravä, please give protection to these
sanskrit:
two lambs, who have fallen down with me. Although I belong to the
heavenly planets and you belong to earth, I shall certainly enjoy sexual
union with you. I have no objection to accepting you as my husband, for
you are superior in every respect.

text: Urvaçé said: "My dear hero, only preparations made in
sanskrit:
ghee [clarified butter] will be my eatables, and I shall not want to see
you naked at any time, except at the time of sexual intercourse." The
great-minded King Purüravä accepted these proposals.

text: Purüravä replied: O beautiful one, your beauty is
sanskrit:
wonderful and your gestures are also wonderful. Indeed, you are
attractive to all human society. Therefore, since you have come of your
own accord from the heavenly planets, who on earth would not agree to
serve a demigoddess such as you.

text: Çukadeva Gosvämé continued: The best of human beings,
sanskrit:
Purüravä, began freely enjoying the company of Urvaçé, who engaged
in sexual activities with him in many celestial places, such as
Caitraratha and Nandana-känana, where the demigods enjoy.

text: Urvaçé's body was as fragrant as the saffron of a lotus.
sanskrit:
Being enlivened by the fragrance of her face and body, Purüravä
enjoyed her company for many days with great jubilation.

text: Not seeing Urvaçé in his assembly, the King of heaven,
sanskrit:
Lord Indra, said, "Without Urvaçé my assembly is no longer beautiful."
Considering this, he requested the Gandharvas to bring her back to his
heavenly planet.

text: Thus the Gandharvas came to earth, and at midnight, when
sanskrit:
everything was dark, they appeared in the house of Purüravä and stole
the two lambs entrusted to the King by his wife, Urvaçé.

text: Urvaçé treated the two lambs like her own sons.
sanskrit:
Therefore, when they were being taken by the Gandharvas and began
crying, Urvaçé heard them and rebuked her husband. "Now I am being
killed," she said, "under the protection of an unworthy husband, who is
a coward and a eunuch although he thinks himself a great hero.

text: "Because I depended on him, the plunderers have deprived me
sanskrit:
of my two sons the lambs, and therefore I am now lost. My husband lies
down at night in fear, exactly like a woman, although he appears to be a
man during the day."

text: Purüravä, stricken by the sharp words of Urvaçé like an
sanskrit:
elephant struck by its driver's pointed rod, became very angry. Not even
dressing himself properly, he took a sword in hand and went out naked
into the night to follow the Gandharvas who had stolen the lambs.

text: After giving up the two lambs, the Gandharvas shone
sanskrit:
brightly like lightning, thus illuminating the house of Purüravä.
Urvaçé then saw her husband returning with the lambs in hand, but he
was naked, and therefore she left.

text: No longer seeing Urvaçé on his bed, Purüravä was most
sanskrit:
aggrieved. Because of his great attraction for her, he was very much
disturbed. Thus, lamenting, he began traveling about the earth like a
madman.

text: Once during his travels all over the world, Purüravä saw
sanskrit:
Urvaçé, accompanied by five companions, on the bank of the Sarasvaté
at Kurukñetra. With jubilation in his face, he then spoke to her in
sweet words as follows.

text: O my dear wife, O most cruel one, kindly stay, kindly stay.
sanskrit:

will fall down here, and because it is unsuitable for your pleasure, it

sanskrit:

text: Çukadeva Gosvämé continued: O King Parékñit, from the
sanskrit:
womb of Urvaçé, six sons were generated by Purüravä. Their names
were Äyu, Çrutäyu, Satyäyu, Raya, Vijaya and Jaya.

text: The son of Çrutäyu was Vasumän; the son of Satyäyu,
sanskrit:
Çrutaïjaya; the son of Raya, Eka; the son of Jaya, Amita; and the son
of Vijaya, Bhéma. The son of Bhéma was Käïcana; the son of Käïcana
was Hotraka; and the son of Hotraka was Jahnu, who drank all the water
of the Ganges in one sip.

text: The son of Jahnu was Puru, the son of Puru was Baläka, the
sanskrit:
son of Baläka was Ajaka, and the son of Ajaka was Kuça. Kuça had four
sons, named Kuçämbu, Tanaya, Vasu and Kuçanäbha. The son of
Kuçämbu was Gädhi.

text: King Gädhi had a daughter named Satyavaté, whom a
sanskrit:
brähmaëa sage named Åcéka requested from the King to be his wife.
King Gädhi, however, regarded Åcéka as an unfit husband for his
daughter, and therefore he told the brähmaëa, "My dear sir, I belong
to the dynasty of Kuça. Because we are aristocratic kñatriyas, you
have to give some dowry for my daughter. Therefore, bring at least one
thousand horses, each as brilliant as moonshine and each having one
black ear, whether right or left."

text: When King Gädhi made this demand, the great sage Åcéka
sanskrit:
could understand the King's mind. Therefore he went to the demigod
Varuëa and brought from him the one thousand horses that Gädhi had
demanded. After delivering these horses, the sage married the King's
beautiful daughter.

text: Thereafter, Åcéka Muni's wife and mother-in-law, each
sanskrit:
desiring a son, requested the Muni to prepare an oblation. Thus Åcéka
Muni prepared one oblation for his wife with a brähmaëa mantra and
another for his mother-in-law with a kñatriya mantra. Then he went out
to bathe.

text: Meanwhile, because Satyavaté's mother thought that the
sanskrit:
oblation prepared for her daughter, Åcéka's wife, must be better, she
asked her daughter for that oblation. Satyavaté therefore gave her own
oblation to her mother and ate her mother's oblation herself.

text: When the great sage Åcéka returned home after bathing and
sanskrit:
understood what had happened in his absence, he said to his wife,
Satyavaté, "You have done a great wrong. Your son will be a fierce
kñatriya, able to punish everyone, and your brother will be a learned
scholar in spiritual science."

text: Satyavaté, however, pacified Åcéka Muni with peaceful
sanskrit:
words and requested that her son not be like a fierce kñatriya. Åcéka
Muni replied, "Then your grandson will be of a kñatriya spirit." Thus
Jamadagni was born as the son of Satyavaté.

text: Satyavaté later became the sacred river Kauçiké to
sanskrit:
purify the entire world, and her son, Jamadagni, married Reëukä, the
daughter of Reëu. By the semen of Jamadagni, many sons, headed by
Vasumän, were born from the womb of Reëukä. The youngest of them was
named Räma, or Paraçuräma.

text: Learned scholars accept this Paraçuräma as the celebrated
sanskrit:
incarnation of Väsudeva who annihilated the dynasty of Kärtavérya.
Paraçuräma killed all the kñatriyas on earth twenty-one times.

text: When the royal dynasty, being excessively proud because of
sanskrit:
the material modes of passion and ignorance, became irreligious and
ceased to care for the laws enacted by the brähmaëas, Paraçuräma
killed them. Although their offense was not very severe, he killed them
to lessen the burden of the world.

text: King Parékñit inquired from Çukadeva Gosvämé: What was
sanskrit:
the offense that the kñatriyas who could not control their senses
committed before Lord Paraçuräma, the incarnation of the Supreme
Personality of Godhead, for which the Lord annihilated the kñatriya
dynasty again and again?

text: Çukadeva Gosvämé said: The best of the kñatriyas,
sanskrit:
Kärtavéryärjuna, the King of the Haihayas, received one thousand arms
by worshiping Dattätreya, the plenary expansion of the Supreme
Personality of Godhead, Näräyaëa. He also became undefeatable by
enemies and received unobstructed sensory power, beauty, influence,
strength, fame and the mystic power by which to achieve all the
perfections of yoga, such as aëimä and laghimä. Thus having become
fully opulent, he roamed all over the universe without opposition, just
like the wind.

text: Once while enjoying in the water of the River Narmadä, the
sanskrit:
puffed-up Kärtavéryärjuna, surrounded by beautiful women and
garlanded with a garland of victory, stopped the flow of the water with
his arms.

text: Because Kärtavéryärjuna made the water flow in the
sanskrit:
opposite direction, the camp of Rävaëa, which was set up on the bank
of the Narmadä near the city of Mähiñmaté, was inundated. This was
unbearable to the ten-headed Rävaëa, who considered himself a great
hero and could not tolerate Kärtavéryärjuna's power.

text: When Rävaëa attempted to insult Kärtavéryärjuna in the
sanskrit:
presence of the women and thus offended him, Kärtavéryärjuna easily
arrested Rävaëa and put him in custody in the city of Mähiñmaté,
just as one captures a monkey, and then released him neglectfully.

text: Once while Kärtavéryärjuna was wandering unengaged in a
sanskrit: solitary forest and hunting, he approached the residence of Jamadagni.

text: The sage Jamadagni, who was engaged in great austerities in
sanskrit:
the forest, received the King very well, along with the King's soldiers,
ministers and carriers. He supplied all the necessities to worship these
guests, for he possessed a kämadhenu cow that was able to supply
everything.

text: Kärtavéryärjuna thought that Jamadagni was more powerful
sanskrit:
and wealthy than himself because of possessing a jewel in the form of
the kämadhenu. Therefore he and his own men, the Haihayas, were not
very much appreciative of Jamadagni's reception. On the contrary, they
wanted to possess that kämadhenu, which was useful for the execution of
the agnihotra sacrifice.

text: Being puffed up by material power, Kärtavéryärjuna
sanskrit:
encouraged his men to steal Jamadagni's kämadhenu. Thus the men
forcibly took away the crying kämadhenu, along with her calf, to
Mähiñmaté, Kärtavéryärjuna's capital.

text: Thereafter, Kärtavéryärjuna having left with the
sanskrit:
kämadhenu, Paraçuräma returned to the äçrama. When Paraçuräma,
the youngest son of Jamadagni, heard about Kärtavéryärjuna's
nefarious deed, he became as angry as a trampled snake.

text: Taking up his fierce chopper, his shield, his bow and a
sanskrit:
quiver of arrows, Lord Paraçuräma, exceedingly angry, chased
Kärtavéryärjuna just as a lion chases an elephant.

text: As King Kärtavéryärjuna entered his capital,
sanskrit:
Mähiñmaté Puré, he saw Lord Paraçuräma, the best of the Bhågu
dynasty, coming after him, holding a chopper, shield, bow and arrows.
Lord Paraçuräma was covered with a black deerskin, and his matted
locks of hair appeared like the sunshine.

text: Upon seeing Paraçuräma, Kärtavéryärjuna immediately
sanskrit:
feared him and sent many elephants, chariots, horses and infantry
soldiers equipped with clubs, swords, arrows, åñöis, çataghnis,
çaktis, and many similar weapons to fight against him.
Kärtavéryärjuna sent seventeen full akñauhiëés of soldiers to
check Paraçuräma. But Lord Paraçuräma alone killed all of them.

text: Lord Paraçuräma, being expert in killing the military
sanskrit:
strength of the enemy, worked with the speed of the mind and the wind,
slicing his enemies with his chopper [paraçu]. Wherever he went, the
enemies fell, their legs, arms and shoulders being severed, their
chariot drivers killed, and their carriers, the elephants and horses all
annihilated.

text: By manipulating his axe and arrows, Lord Paraçuräma cut
sanskrit:
to pieces the shields, flags, bows and bodies of Kärtavéryärjuna's
soldiers, who fell on the battlefield, muddying the ground with their
blood. Seeing these reverses, Kärtavéryärjuna, infuriated, rushed to
the battlefield.

text: Then Kärtavéryärjuna, with his one thousand arms,
sanskrit:
simultaneously fixed arrows on five hundred bows to kill Lord
Paraçuräma. But Lord Paraçuräma, the best of fighters, released
enough arrows with only one bow to cut to pieces immediately all the
arrows and bows in the hands of Kärtavéryärjuna.

text: When his arrows were cut to pieces, Kärtavéryärjuna
sanskrit:
uprooted many trees and hills with his own hands and again rushed
strongly toward Lord Paraçuräma to kill him. But Paraçuräma then
used his axe with great force to cut off Kärtavéryärjuna's arms, just
as one might lop off the hoods of a serpent.

text: Thereafter, Paraçuräma cut off like a mountain peak
sanskrit:
the head of Kärtavéryärjuna, who had already lost his arms. When

fled in fear. Then Paraçuräma, having killed the enemy, released the

with its calf to his residence, where he gave it to his father,
Jamadagni.

sanskrit:
activities in killing Kärtavéryärjuna. Upon hearing of these deeds,
Jamadagni spoke to his son as follows.

sanskrit:
unnecessarily killed the king, who is supposed to be the embodiment of
all the demigods. Thus you have committed a sin.

text: My dear son, we are all brähmaëas and have become
sanskrit:
worshipable for the people in general because of our quality of
forgiveness. It is because of this quality that Lord Brahmä, the
supreme spiritual master of this universe, has achieved his post.

text: The duty of a brähmaëa is to culture the quality of
sanskrit:
forgiveness, which is illuminating like the sun. The Supreme Personality
of Godhead, Hari, is pleased with those who are forgiving.

text: My dear son, killing a king who is an emperor is more
sanskrit:
severely sinful than killing a brähmaëa. But now, if you become
Kåñëa conscious and worship the holy places, you can atone for this
great sin.

sanskrit:
womb of Urvaçé, six sons were generated by Purüravä. Their names
were Äyu, Çrutäyu, Satyäyu, Raya, Vijaya and Jaya.

text: The son of Çrutäyu was Vasumän; the son of Satyäyu,
sanskrit:
Çrutaïjaya; the son of Raya, Eka; the son of Jaya, Amita; and the son
of Vijaya, Bhéma. The son of Bhéma was Käïcana; the son of Käïcana
was Hotraka; and the son of Hotraka was Jahnu, who drank all the water
of the Ganges in one sip.

text: The son of Jahnu was Puru, the son of Puru was Baläka, the
sanskrit:
son of Baläka was Ajaka, and the son of Ajaka was Kuça. Kuça had four
sons, named Kuçämbu, Tanaya, Vasu and Kuçanäbha. The son of
Kuçämbu was Gädhi.

text: King Gädhi had a daughter named Satyavaté, whom a
sanskrit:
brähmaëa sage named Åcéka requested from the King to be his wife.
King Gädhi, however, regarded Åcéka as an unfit husband for his
daughter, and therefore he told the brähmaëa, "My dear sir, I belong
to the dynasty of Kuça. Because we are aristocratic kñatriyas, you
have to give some dowry for my daughter. Therefore, bring at least one
thousand horses, each as brilliant as moonshine and each having one
black ear, whether right or left."

text: When King Gädhi made this demand, the great sage Åcéka
sanskrit:
could understand the King's mind. Therefore he went to the demigod
Varuëa and brought from him the one thousand horses that Gädhi had
demanded. After delivering these horses, the sage married the King's
beautiful daughter.

text: Thereafter, Åcéka Muni's wife and mother-in-law, each
sanskrit:
desiring a son, requested the Muni to prepare an oblation. Thus Åcéka
Muni prepared one oblation for his wife with a brähmaëa mantra and
another for his mother-in-law with a kñatriya mantra. Then he went out
to bathe.

text: Meanwhile, because Satyavaté's mother thought that the
sanskrit:
oblation prepared for her daughter, Åcéka's wife, must be better, she
asked her daughter for that oblation. Satyavaté therefore gave her own
oblation to her mother and ate her mother's oblation herself.

text: When the great sage Åcéka returned home after bathing and
sanskrit:
understood what had happened in his absence, he said to his wife,
Satyavaté, "You have done a great wrong. Your son will be a fierce
kñatriya, able to punish everyone, and your brother will be a learned
scholar in spiritual science."

text: Satyavaté, however, pacified Åcéka Muni with peaceful
sanskrit:
words and requested that her son not be like a fierce kñatriya. Åcéka
Muni replied, "Then your grandson will be of a kñatriya spirit." Thus
Jamadagni was born as the son of Satyavaté.

text: Satyavaté later became the sacred river Kauçiké to
sanskrit:
purify the entire world, and her son, Jamadagni, married Reëukä, the
daughter of Reëu. By the semen of Jamadagni, many sons, headed by
Vasumän, were born from the womb of Reëukä. The youngest of them was
named Räma, or Paraçuräma.

text: Learned scholars accept this Paraçuräma as the celebrated
sanskrit:
incarnation of Väsudeva who annihilated the dynasty of Kärtavérya.
Paraçuräma killed all the kñatriyas on earth twenty-one times.

text: When the royal dynasty, being excessively proud because of
sanskrit:
the material modes of passion and ignorance, became irreligious and
ceased to care for the laws enacted by the brähmaëas, Paraçuräma
killed them. Although their offense was not very severe, he killed them
to lessen the burden of the world.

text: King Parékñit inquired from Çukadeva Gosvämé: What was
sanskrit:
the offense that the kñatriyas who could not control their senses
committed before Lord Paraçuräma, the incarnation of the Supreme
Personality of Godhead, for which the Lord annihilated the kñatriya
dynasty again and again?

text: Çukadeva Gosvämé said: The best of the kñatriyas,
sanskrit:
Kärtavéryärjuna, the King of the Haihayas, received one thousand arms
by worshiping Dattätreya, the plenary expansion of the Supreme
Personality of Godhead, Näräyaëa. He also became undefeatable by
enemies and received unobstructed sensory power, beauty, influence,
strength, fame and the mystic power by which to achieve all the
perfections of yoga, such as aëimä and laghimä. Thus having become
fully opulent, he roamed all over the universe without opposition, just
like the wind.

text: Once while enjoying in the water of the River Narmadä, the
sanskrit:
puffed-up Kärtavéryärjuna, surrounded by beautiful women and
garlanded with a garland of victory, stopped the flow of the water with
his arms.

text: Because Kärtavéryärjuna made the water flow in the
sanskrit:
opposite direction, the camp of Rävaëa, which was set up on the bank
of the Narmadä near the city of Mähiñmaté, was inundated. This was
unbearable to the ten-headed Rävaëa, who considered himself a great
hero and could not tolerate Kärtavéryärjuna's power.

text: When Rävaëa attempted to insult Kärtavéryärjuna in the
sanskrit:
presence of the women and thus offended him, Kärtavéryärjuna easily
arrested Rävaëa and put him in custody in the city of Mähiñmaté,
just as one captures a monkey, and then released him neglectfully.

text: Once while Kärtavéryärjuna was wandering unengaged in a
sanskrit: solitary forest and hunting, he approached the residence of Jamadagni.

text: The sage Jamadagni, who was engaged in great austerities in
sanskrit:
the forest, received the King very well, along with the King's soldiers,
ministers and carriers. He supplied all the necessities to worship these
guests, for he possessed a kämadhenu cow that was able to supply
everything.

text: Kärtavéryärjuna thought that Jamadagni was more powerful
sanskrit:
and wealthy than himself because of possessing a jewel in the form of
the kämadhenu. Therefore he and his own men, the Haihayas, were not
very much appreciative of Jamadagni's reception. On the contrary, they
wanted to possess that kämadhenu, which was useful for the execution of
the agnihotra sacrifice.

text: Being puffed up by material power, Kärtavéryärjuna
sanskrit:
encouraged his men to steal Jamadagni's kämadhenu. Thus the men
forcibly took away the crying kämadhenu, along with her calf, to
Mähiñmaté, Kärtavéryärjuna's capital.

text: Thereafter, Kärtavéryärjuna having left with the
sanskrit:
kämadhenu, Paraçuräma returned to the äçrama. When Paraçuräma,
the youngest son of Jamadagni, heard about Kärtavéryärjuna's
nefarious deed, he became as angry as a trampled snake.

text: Taking up his fierce chopper, his shield, his bow and a
sanskrit:
quiver of arrows, Lord Paraçuräma, exceedingly angry, chased
Kärtavéryärjuna just as a lion chases an elephant.

text: As King Kärtavéryärjuna entered his capital,
sanskrit:
Mähiñmaté Puré, he saw Lord Paraçuräma, the best of the Bhågu
dynasty, coming after him, holding a chopper, shield, bow and arrows.
Lord Paraçuräma was covered with a black deerskin, and his matted
locks of hair appeared like the sunshine.

text: Upon seeing Paraçuräma, Kärtavéryärjuna immediately
sanskrit:
feared him and sent many elephants, chariots, horses and infantry
soldiers equipped with clubs, swords, arrows, åñöis, çataghnis,
çaktis, and many similar weapons to fight against him.
Kärtavéryärjuna sent seventeen full akñauhiëés of soldiers to
check Paraçuräma. But Lord Paraçuräma alone killed all of them.

text: Lord Paraçuräma, being expert in killing the military
sanskrit:
strength of the enemy, worked with the speed of the mind and the wind,
slicing his enemies with his chopper [paraçu]. Wherever he went, the
enemies fell, their legs, arms and shoulders being severed, their
chariot drivers killed, and their carriers, the elephants and horses all
annihilated.

text: By manipulating his axe and arrows, Lord Paraçuräma cut
sanskrit:
to pieces the shields, flags, bows and bodies of Kärtavéryärjuna's
soldiers, who fell on the battlefield, muddying the ground with their
blood. Seeing these reverses, Kärtavéryärjuna, infuriated, rushed to
the battlefield.

text: Then Kärtavéryärjuna, with his one thousand arms,
sanskrit:
simultaneously fixed arrows on five hundred bows to kill Lord
Paraçuräma. But Lord Paraçuräma, the best of fighters, released
enough arrows with only one bow to cut to pieces immediately all the
arrows and bows in the hands of Kärtavéryärjuna.

text: When his arrows were cut to pieces, Kärtavéryärjuna
sanskrit:
uprooted many trees and hills with his own hands and again rushed
strongly toward Lord Paraçuräma to kill him. But Paraçuräma then
used his axe with great force to cut off Kärtavéryärjuna's arms, just
as one might lop off the hoods of a serpent.

text: Thereafter, Paraçuräma cut off like a mountain peak
sanskrit:
the head of Kärtavéryärjuna, who had already lost his arms. When

sanskrit:
of the Kuru dynasty, when Lord Paraçuräma was given this order by his
father, he immediately agreed, saying, "Let it be so." For one complete
year he traveled to holy places. Then he returned to his father's
residence.

text: Once when Reëukä, the wife of Jamadagni, went to the bank
sanskrit:
of the Ganges to get water, she saw the King of the Gandharvas,
decorated with a garland of lotuses and sporting in the Ganges with
celestial women [Apsaräs].

text: She had gone to bring water from the Ganges, but when she
sanskrit:
saw Citraratha, the King of the Gandharvas, sporting with the celestial
girls, she was somewhat inclined toward him and failed to remember that
the time for the fire sacrifice was passing.

text: Later, understanding that the time for offering the
sanskrit:
sacrifice had passed, Reëukä feared a curse from her husband.
Therefore when she returned she simply put the waterpot before him and
stood there with folded hands.

text: The great sage Jamadagni understood the adultery in the mind
sanskrit:
of his wife. Therefore he was very angry and told his sons, "My dear
sons, kill this sinful woman!" But the sons did not carry out his order.

text: Jamadagni then ordered his youngest son, Paraçuräma, to
sanskrit:
kill his brothers, who had disobeyed this order, and his mother, who had
mentally committed adultery. Lord Paraçuräma, knowing the power of his
father, who was practiced in meditation and austerity, killed his mother
and brothers immediately.

text: Jamadagni, the son of Satyavaté, was very much pleased with
sanskrit:
Paraçuräma and asked him to take any benediction he liked. Lord
Paraçuräma replied, "Let my mother and brothers live again and not
remember having been killed by me. This is the benediction I ask."

text: Thereafter, by the benediction of Jamadagni, Lord
sanskrit:
Paraçuräma's mother and brothers immediately came alive and were very
happy, as if awakened from sound sleep. Lord Paraçuräma had killed his
relatives in accordance with his father's order because he was fully
aware of his father's power, austerity and learning.

text: My dear King Parékñit, the sons of Kärtavéryärjuna, who
sanskrit:
were defeated by the superior strength of Paraçuräma, never achieved
happiness, for they always remembered the killing of their father.

text: Once when Paraçuräma left the äçrama for the forest
sanskrit:
with Vasumän and his other brothers, the sons of Kärtavéryärjuna
took the opportunity to approach Jamadagni's residence to seek vengeance
for their grudge.

text: The sons of Kärtavéryärjuna were determined to commit
sanskrit:
sinful deeds. Therefore when they saw Jamadagni sitting by the side of
the fire to perform yajïa and meditating upon the Supreme Personality
of Godhead, who is praised by the best of selected prayers, they took
the opportunity to kill him.

text: With pitiable prayers, Reëukä, the mother of Paraçuräma
sanskrit:
and wife of Jamadagni, begged for the life of her husband. But the sons
of Kärtavéryärjuna, being devoid of the qualities of kñatriyas, were
so cruel that despite her prayers they forcibly cut off his head and
took it away.

text: Lamenting in grief for the death of her husband, the most
sanskrit:
chaste Reëukä struck her own body with her hands and cried very
loudly, "O Räma, my dear son Räma!"

text: Although the sons of Jamadagni, including Lord
sanskrit:
Paraçuräma, were a long distance from home, as soon as they heard
Reëukä loudly calling "O Räma, O my son," they hastily returned to
the äçrama, where they saw their father already killed.

text: Virtually bewildered by grief, anger, indignation,
sanskrit:
affliction and lamentation, the sons of Jamadagni cried, "O father, most
religious, saintly person, you have left us and gone to the heavenly
planets !"

text: Thus lamenting, Lord Paraçuräma entrusted his father's
sanskrit:
dead body to his brothers and personally took up his axe, having decided
to put an end to all the kñatriyas on the surface of the world.

sanskrit:
was already doomed by the sinful killing of a brähmaëa. In the midst

sons of Kärtavéryärjuna.

text: With the blood of the bodies of these sons, Lord
sanskrit:
Paraçuräma created a ghastly river, which brought great fear to the
kings who had no respect for brahminical culture. Because the
kñatriyas, the men of power in government, were performing sinful
activities, Lord Paraçuräma, on the plea of retaliating for the murder
of his father, rid all the kñatriyas from the face of the earth
twenty-one times. Indeed, in the place known as Samanta-païcaka he
created nine lakes filled with their blood.

text: Thereafter, Paraçuräma joined his father's head to the
sanskrit:
dead body and placed the whole body and head upon kuça grass. By
offering sacrifices, he began to worship Lord Väsudeva, who is the
all-pervading Supersoul of all the demigods and of every living entity.

text: After completing the sacrifice, Lord Paraçuräma gave
sanskrit:
the eastern direction to the hotä as a gift, the south to the brahmä,
the west to the adhvaryu, the north to the udgätä, and the four
corners-northeast, southeast, northwest and southwest-to the other
priests. He gave the middle to Kaçyapa and the place known as
Äryävarta to the upadrañöä. Whatever remained he distributed among
the sadasyas, the associate priests.

text: Thereafter, having completed the ritualistic sacrificial
sanskrit:
ceremonies, Lord Paraçuräma took the bath known as the
avabhåtha-snäna. Standing on the bank of the great river Sarasvaté,
cleared of all sins, Lord Paraçuräma appeared like the sun in a clear,
cloudless sky.

text: Thus Jamadagni, being worshiped by Lord Paraçuräma, was
sanskrit:
brought back to life with full remembrance, and he became one of the
seven sages in the group of seven stars.

text: My dear King Parékñit, in the next manvantara the
sanskrit:
lotus-eyed Personality of Godhead Lord Paraçuräma, the son of
Jamadagni, will be a great propounder of Vedic knowledge. In other
words, he will be one of the seven sages.

text: Lord Paraçuräma still lives as an intelligent brähmaëa
sanskrit:
in the mountainous country known as Mahendra. Completely satisfied,
having given up all the weapons of a kñatriya, he is always worshiped,
adored and offered prayers for his exalted character and activities by
such celestial beings as the Siddhas, Cäraëas and Gandharvas.

text: In this way the supreme soul, the Supreme Personality of
sanskrit:
Godhead, the Lord and the supreme controller, descended as an
incarnation in the Bhågu dynasty and released the universe from the
burden of undesirable kings by killing them many times.

text: Viçvämitra, the son of Mahäräja Gädhi, was as powerful
sanskrit:
as the flames of fire. From the position of a kñatriya, he achieved the
position of a powerful brähmaëa by undergoing penances and
austerities.

text: O King Parékñit, Viçvämitra had 101 sons, of whom the
sanskrit:
middle one was known as Madhucchandä. In relation to him, all the other
sons were celebrated as the Madhucchandäs.

text: Viçvämitra accepted the son of Ajégarta known as
sanskrit:
Çunaùçepha, who was born in the Bhågu dynasty and was also known as
Devaräta, as one of his own sons. Viçvämitra ordered his other sons
to accept Çunaùçepha as their eldest brother.

text: Çunaùçepha's father sold Çunaùçepha to be sacrificed
sanskrit:
as a man-animal in the yajïa of King Hariçcandra. When Çunaùçepha
was brought into the sacrificial arena, he prayed to the demigods for
release and was released by their mercy.

text: Although Çunaùçepha was born in the Bhärgava dynasty,
sanskrit:
he was greatly advanced in spiritual life, and therefore the demigods
involved in the sacrifice protected him. Consequently he was also
celebrated as the descendant of Gädhi named Devaräta.

text: When requested by their father to accept Çunaùçepha as
sanskrit:
the eldest son, the elder fifty of the Madhucchandäs, the sons of
Viçvämitra, did not agree. Therefore Viçvämitra, being angry, cursed
them. "May all of you bad sons become mlecchas," he said, "being opposed
to the principles of Vedic culture."

text: When the elder Madhucchandäs were cursed, the younger
sanskrit:
fifty, along with Madhucchandä himself, approached their father and
agreed to accept his proposal. "Dear father," they said, "we shall abide
by whatever arrangement you like."

text: Thus the younger Madhucchandäs accepted Çunaùçepha as
sanskrit:
their eldest brother and told him, "We shall follow your orders."
Viçvämitra then said to his obedient sons, "Because you have accepted
Çunaùçepha as your eldest brother, I am very satisfied. By accepting
my order, you have made me a father of worthy sons, and therefore I
bless all of you to become the fathers of sons also."

text: Viçvämitra said, "O Kuçikas [descendants of Kauçika],
sanskrit:
this Devaräta is my son and is one of you. Please obey his orders." O
King Parékñit, Viçvämitra had many other sons, such as Añöaka,
Häréta, Jaya and Kratumän.

text: Viçvämitra cursed some of his sons and blessed the
sanskrit:
others, and he also adopted a son. Thus there were varieties in the
Kauçika dynasty, but among all the sons, Devaräta was considered the
eldest.

text: Çukadeva Gosvämé said: My dear Mahäräja Parékñit, son
sanskrit:
of the Kuru dynasty, when Lord Paraçuräma was given this order by his
father, he immediately agreed, saying, "Let it be so." For one complete
year he traveled to holy places. Then he returned to his father's
residence.

text: Once when Reëukä, the wife of Jamadagni, went to the bank
sanskrit:
of the Ganges to get water, she saw the King of the Gandharvas,
decorated with a garland of lotuses and sporting in the Ganges with
celestial women [Apsaräs].

text: She had gone to bring water from the Ganges, but when she
sanskrit:
saw Citraratha, the King of the Gandharvas, sporting with the celestial
girls, she was somewhat inclined toward him and failed to remember that
the time for the fire sacrifice was passing.

text: Later, understanding that the time for offering the
sanskrit:
sacrifice had passed, Reëukä feared a curse from her husband.
Therefore when she returned she simply put the waterpot before him and
stood there with folded hands.

text: The great sage Jamadagni understood the adultery in the mind
sanskrit:
of his wife. Therefore he was very angry and told his sons, "My dear
sons, kill this sinful woman!" But the sons did not carry out his order.

text: Jamadagni then ordered his youngest son, Paraçuräma, to
sanskrit:
kill his brothers, who had disobeyed this order, and his mother, who had
mentally committed adultery. Lord Paraçuräma, knowing the power of his
father, who was practiced in meditation and austerity, killed his mother
and brothers immediately.

text: Jamadagni, the son of Satyavaté, was very much pleased with
sanskrit:
Paraçuräma and asked him to take any benediction he liked. Lord
Paraçuräma replied, "Let my mother and brothers live again and not
remember having been killed by me. This is the benediction I ask."

text: Thereafter, by the benediction of Jamadagni, Lord
sanskrit:
Paraçuräma's mother and brothers immediately came alive and were very
happy, as if awakened from sound sleep. Lord Paraçuräma had killed his
relatives in accordance with his father's order because he was fully
aware of his father's power, austerity and learning.

text: My dear King Parékñit, the sons of Kärtavéryärjuna, who
sanskrit:
were defeated by the superior strength of Paraçuräma, never achieved
happiness, for they always remembered the killing of their father.

text: Once when Paraçuräma left the äçrama for the forest
sanskrit:
with Vasumän and his other brothers, the sons of Kärtavéryärjuna
took the opportunity to approach Jamadagni's residence to seek vengeance
for their grudge.

text: The sons of Kärtavéryärjuna were determined to commit
sanskrit:
sinful deeds. Therefore when they saw Jamadagni sitting by the side of
the fire to perform yajïa and meditating upon the Supreme Personality
of Godhead, who is praised by the best of selected prayers, they took
the opportunity to kill him.

text: With pitiable prayers, Reëukä, the mother of Paraçuräma
sanskrit:
and wife of Jamadagni, begged for the life of her husband. But the sons
of Kärtavéryärjuna, being devoid of the qualities of kñatriyas, were
so cruel that despite her prayers they forcibly cut off his head and
took it away.

text: Lamenting in grief for the death of her husband, the most
sanskrit:
chaste Reëukä struck her own body with her hands and cried very
loudly, "O Räma, my dear son Räma!"

text: Although the sons of Jamadagni, including Lord
sanskrit:
Paraçuräma, were a long distance from home, as soon as they heard
Reëukä loudly calling "O Räma, O my son," they hastily returned to
the äçrama, where they saw their father already killed.

text: Virtually bewildered by grief, anger, indignation,
sanskrit:
affliction and lamentation, the sons of Jamadagni cried, "O father, most
religious, saintly person, you have left us and gone to the heavenly
planets !"

sanskrit:

text: Çukadeva Gosvämé said: From Purüravä came a son named
sanskrit:
Äyu, whose very powerful sons were Nahuña, Kñatravåddha, Rajé,
Räbha and Anenä. O Mahäräja Parékñit, now hear about the dynasty
of Kñatravåddha. Kñatravåddha's son was Suhotra, who had three sons,
named Käçya, Kuça and Gåtsamada. From Gåtsamada came Çunaka, and
from him came Çaunaka, the great saint, the best of those conversant
with the Åg Veda.

text: The son of Käçya was Käçi, and his son was Räñöra,
sanskrit:
the father of Dérghatama. Dérghatama had a son named Dhanvantari, who
was the inaugurator of the medical science and an incarnation of Lord
Väsudeva, the enjoyer of the results of sacrifices. One who remembers
the name of Dhanvantari can be released from all disease.

text: The son of Dhanvantari was Ketumän, and his son was
sanskrit:
Bhémaratha. The son of Bhémaratha was Divodäsa, and the son of
Divodäsa was Dyumän, also known as Pratardana.

text: Dyumän was also known as Çatrujit, Vatsa, Åtadhvaja and
sanskrit: Kuvalayäçva. From him were born Alarka and other sons.

text: Alarka, the son of Dyumän, reigned over the earth for
sanskrit:
sixty-six thousand years, my dear King Parékñit. No one other than him
has reigned over the earth for so long as a young man.

text: From Alarka came a son named Santati, and his son was
sanskrit:
Sunétha. The son of Sunétha was Niketana, the son of Niketana was
Dharmaketu, and the son of Dharmaketu was Satyaketu.

text: O King Parékñit, from Satyaketu came a son named
sanskrit:
Dhåñöaketu, and from Dhåñöaketu came Sukumära, the emperor of the
entire world. From Sukumära came a son named Vétihotra; from
Vétihotra, Bharga; and from Bharga, Bhärgabhümi.

text: O Mahäräja Parékñit, all of these kings were
sanskrit:
descendants of Käçi, and they could also be called descendants of
Kñatravåddha. The son of Räbha was Rabhasa, from Rabhasa came
Gambhéra, and from Gambhéra came a son named Akriya.

text: The son of Akriya was known as Brahmavit, O King. Now hear
sanskrit:
about the descendants of Anenä. From Anenä came a son named Çuddha,
and his son was Çuci. The son of Çuci was Dharmasärathi, also called
Citrakåt.

text: From Citrakåt was born a son named Çäntaraja, a
sanskrit:
self-realized soul who performed all kinds of Vedic ritualistic
ceremonies and therefore did not beget any progeny. The sons of Rajé
were five hundred, all very powerful.

text: On the request of the demigods, Rajé killed the demons and
sanskrit:
thus returned the kingdom of heaven to Lord Indra. But Indra, fearing
such demons as Prahläda, returned the kingdom of heaven to Rajé and
surrendered himself at Rajé's lotus feet.

text: Upon Rajé's death, Indra begged Rajé's sons for the
sanskrit:
return of the heavenly planet. They did not return it, however, although
they agreed to return Indra's shares in ritualistic ceremonies.

text: Thereafter, Båhaspati, the spiritual master of the
sanskrit:
demigods, offered oblations in the fire so that the sons of Rajé would
fall from moral principles. When they fell, Lord Indra killed them
easily because of their degradation. Not a single one of them remained
alive.

text: From Kuça, the grandson of Kñatravåddha, was born a son
sanskrit:
named Prati. The son of Prati was Saïjaya, and the son of Saïjaya was
Jaya. From Jaya, Kåta was born, and from Kåta, King Haryabala.

text: From Haryabala came a son named Sahadeva, and from Sahadeva
sanskrit:
came Héna. The son of Héna was Jayasena, and the son of Jayasena was
Saìkåti. The son of Saìkåti was the powerful and expert fighter
named Jaya. These kings were the members of the Kñatravåddha dynasty.
Now let me describe to you the dynasty of Nahuña.

text: Çukadeva Gosvämé said: From Purüravä came a son named
sanskrit:
Äyu, whose very powerful sons were Nahuña, Kñatravåddha, Rajé,
Räbha and Anenä. O Mahäräja Parékñit, now hear about the dynasty
of Kñatravåddha. Kñatravåddha's son was Suhotra, who had three sons,
named Käçya, Kuça and Gåtsamada. From Gåtsamada came Çunaka, and
from him came Çaunaka, the great saint, the best of those conversant
with the Åg Veda.

text: The son of Käçya was Käçi, and his son was Räñöra,
sanskrit:
the father of Dérghatama. Dérghatama had a son named Dhanvantari, who
was the inaugurator of the medical science and an incarnation of Lord

the name of Dhanvantari can be released from all disease.

text: The son of Dhanvantari was Ketumän, and his son was
sanskrit:
Bhémaratha. The son of Bhémaratha was Divodäsa, and the son of
Divodäsa was Dyumän, also known as Pratardana.

text: Dyumän was also known as Çatrujit, Vatsa, Åtadhvaja and
sanskrit: Kuvalayäçva. From him were born Alarka and other sons.

text: Alarka, the son of Dyumän, reigned over the earth for
sanskrit:
sixty-six thousand years, my dear King Parékñit. No one other than him
has reigned over the earth for so long as a young man.

text: From Alarka came a son named Santati, and his son was
sanskrit:
Sunétha. The son of Sunétha was Niketana, the son of Niketana was

sanskrit:

sanskrit:

Now let me describe to you the dynasty of Nahuña.

text: Çukadeva Gosvämé said: O King Parékñit, as the embodied
sanskrit:
soul has six senses, King Nahuña had six sons, named Yati, Yayäti,
Saàyäti, Äyati, Viyati and Kåti.

text: When one enters the post of king or head of the government,
sanskrit:
one cannot understand the meaning of self-realization. Knowing this,
Yati, the eldest son of Nahuña, did not accept the power to rule,
although it was offered by his father.

text: Because Nahuña, the father of Yayäti, molested Indra's
sanskrit:
wife, Çacé, who then complained to Agastya and other brähmaëas,
these saintly brähmaëas cursed Nahuña to fall from the heavenly
planets and be degraded to the status of a python. Consequently, Yayäti
became the king.

text: King Yayäti had four younger brothers, whom he allowed to
sanskrit:
rule the four directions. Yayäti himself married Devayäné, the
daughter of Çukräcärya, and Çarmiñöhä, the daughter of
Våñaparvä, and ruled the entire earth.

text: Mahäräja Parékñit said: Çukräcärya was a very
sanskrit:
powerful brähmaëa, and Mahäräja Yayäti was a kñatriya. Therefore I
am curious to know how there occurred this pratiloma marriage between a
kñatriya and a brähmaëa.

text: Çukadeva Gosvämé said: One day Våñaparvä's daughter
sanskrit:
Çarmiñöhä, who was innocent but angry by nature, was walking with
Devayäné, the daughter of Çukräcärya, and with thousands of
friends, in the palace garden. The garden was full of lotuses and trees
of flowers and fruits and was inhabited by sweetly singing birds and
bumblebees.

text: When the young, lotus-eyed girls came to the bank of a
sanskrit:
reservoir of water, they wanted to enjoy by bathing. Thus they left
their clothing on the bank and began sporting, throwing water on one
another.

text: While sporting in the water, the girls suddenly saw Lord
sanskrit:
Çiva passing by, seated on the back of his bull with his wife,
Pärvaté. Ashamed because they were naked, the girls quickly got out of
the water and covered themselves with their garments.

text: Çarmiñöhä unknowingly put Devayäné's dress on her own
sanskrit: body, thus angering Devayäné, who then spoke as follows.

text: Oh, just see the activities of this servant-maid
sanskrit:
Çarmiñöhä! Disregarding all etiquette, she has put on my dress, just
like a dog snatching clarified butter meant for use in a sacrifice.

text: We are among the qualified brähmaëas, who are accepted
sanskrit:
as the face of the Supreme Personality of Godhead. The brähmaëas have
created the entire universe by their austerity, and they always keep the
Absolute Truth within the core of their hearts. They have directed the
path of good fortune, the path of Vedic civilization, and because they
are the only worshipable objects within this world, they are offered
prayers and worshiped even by the great demigods, the directors of the
various planets, and even by the Supreme Personality of Godhead, the
Supersoul, the supreme purifier, the husband of the goddess of fortune.
And we are even more respectable because we are in the dynasty of
Bhågu. Yet although this woman's father, being among the demons, is our
disciple, she has put on my dress, exactly like a çüdra taking charge
of Vedic knowledge.

text: Çukadeva Gosvämé said: When thus rebuked in cruel words,
sanskrit:
Çarmiñöhä was very angry. Breathing heavily like a serpent and
biting her lower lip with her teeth, she spoke to the daughter of
Çukräcärya as follows.

text: You beggar, since you don't understand your position, why
sanskrit:
should you unnecessarily talk so much? Don't all of you wait at our
house, depending on us for your livelihood like crows?

text: Using such unkind words, Çarmiñöhä rebuked Devayäné,
sanskrit:
the daughter of Çukräcärya. In anger, she took away Devayäné's
garments and threw Devayäné into a well.

text: After throwing Devayäné into the well, Çarmiñöhä went
sanskrit:
home. Meanwhile, King Yayäti, while engaged in a hunting excursion,
went to the well to drink water and by chance saw Devayäné.

text: Seeing Devayäné naked in the well, King Yayäti
sanskrit:
immediately gave her his upper cloth. Being very kind to her, he caught
her hand with his own and lifted her out.

text: With words saturated with love and affection, Devayäné
sanskrit:
said to King Yayäti: O great hero, O King, conqueror of the cities of
your enemies, by accepting my hand you have accepted me as your married
wife. Let me not be touched by others, for our relationship as husband
and wife has been made possible by providence, not by any human being.

text: Because of falling in the well, I met you. Indeed, this has
sanskrit:
been arranged by providence. After I cursed Kaca, the son of the learned
scholar Båhaspati, he cursed me by saying that I would not have a
brähmaëa for a husband. Therefore, O mighty-armed one, there is no
possibility of my becoming the wife of a brähmaëa.

text: Çukadeva Gosvämé continued: Because such a marriage is
sanskrit:
not sanctioned by regular scriptures, King Yayäti did not like it, but
because it was arranged by providence and because he was attracted by
Devayäné's beauty, he accepted her request.

text: Thereafter, when the learned King returned to his palace,
sanskrit:
Devayäné returned home crying and told her father, Çukräcärya,
about all that had happened because of Çarmiñöhä. She told how she
had been thrown into the well but was saved by the King.

text: As Çukräcärya listened to what had happened to
sanskrit:
Devayäné, his mind was very much aggrieved. Condemning the profession
of priesthood and praising the profession of uïcha-våtti [collecting
grains from the fields], he left home with his daughter.

text: King Våñaparvä understood that Çukräcärya was coming
sanskrit:
to chastise or curse him. Consequently, before Çukräcärya came to his
house, Våñaparvä went out and fell down in the street at the feet of
his guru and satisfied him, checking his wrath.

text: The powerful Çukräcärya was angry for a few moments, but
sanskrit:
upon being satisfied he said to Våñaparvä: My dear King, kindly
fulfill the desire of Devayäné, for she is my daughter and in this
world I cannot give her up or neglect her.

text: After hearing Çukräcärya's request, Våñaparvä agreed
sanskrit:
to fulfill Devayäné's desire, and he awaited her words. Devayäné
then expressed her desire as follows: "Whenever I marry by the order of
my father, my friend Çarmiñöhä must go with me as my maidservant,
along with her friends."

text: Våñaparvä wisely thought that Çukräcärya's
sanskrit:
displeasure would bring danger and that his pleasure would bring
material gain. Therefore he carried out Çukräcärya's order and served
him like a slave. He gave his daughter Çarmiñöhä to Devayäné, and
Çarmiñöhä served Devayäné like a slave, along with thousands of
other women.

text: When Çukräcärya gave Devayäné in marriage to Yayäti,
sanskrit:
he had Çarmiñöhä go with her, but he warned the King, "My dear King,
never allow this girl Çarmiñöhä to lie with you in your bed."

text: O King Parékñit, upon seeing Devayäné with a nice son,
sanskrit:
Çarmiñöhä once approached King Yayäti at the appropriate time for
conception. In a secluded place, she requested the King, the husband of
her friend Devayäné, to enable her to have a son also.

text: When Princess Çarmiñöhä begged King Yayäti for a son,
sanskrit:
the King was certainly aware of the principles of religion, and
therefore he agreed to fulfill her desire. Although he remembered the
warning of Çukräcärya, he thought of this union as the desire of the
Supreme, and thus he had sex with Çarmiñöhä.

text: Devayäné gave birth to Yadu and Turvasu, and
sanskrit: Çarmiñöhä gave birth to Druhyu, Anu and Püru.

text: When the proud Devayäné understood from outside sources
sanskrit:
that Çarmiñöhä was pregnant by her husband, she was frenzied with
anger. Thus she departed for her father's house.

text: King Yayäti, who was very lusty, followed his wife, caught
sanskrit:
her and tried to appease her by speaking pleasing words and massaging
her feet, but he could not satisfy her by any means.

text: Çukräcärya was extremely angry. "You untruthful fool,
sanskrit:
lusting after women! You have done a great wrong," he said. "I therefore
curse you to be attacked and disfigured by old age and invalidity."

text: King Yayäti said, "O learned, worshipable brähmaëa, I
sanskrit:
have not yet satisfied my lusty desires with your daughter."
Çukräcärya then replied, "You may exchange your old age with someone
who will agree to transfer his youth to you."

text: When Yayäti received this benediction from Çukräcärya,
sanskrit:
he requested his eldest son: My dear son Yadu, please give me your youth
in exchange for my old age and invalidity.

text: My dear son, I am not yet satisfied in my sexual desires.
sanskrit:
But if you are kind to me, you can take the old age given by your
maternal grandfather, and I may take your youth so that I may enjoy life
for a few years more.

text: Yadu replied: My dear father, you have already achieved old
sanskrit:
age, although you also were a young man. But I do not welcome your old
age and invalidity, for unless one enjoys material happiness, one cannot
attain renunciation.

text: O Mahäräja Parékñit, Yayäti similarly requested his
sanskrit:
sons Turvasu, Druhyu and Anu to exchange their youth for his old age,
but because they were unaware of religious principles, they thought that
their flickering youth was eternal, and therefore they refused to carry
out their father's order.

text: King Yayäti then requested Püru, who was younger than
sanskrit:
these three brothers but more qualified, "My dear son, do not be
disobedient like your elder brothers, for that is not your duty."

text: Püru replied: O Your Majesty, who in this world can repay
sanskrit:
his debt to his father? By the mercy of one's father, one gets the human
form of life, which can enable one to become an associate of the Supreme
Lord.

text: A son who acts by anticipating what his father wants him to
sanskrit:
do is first class, one who acts upon receiving his father's order is
second class, and one who executes his father's order irreverently is
third class. But a son who refuses his father's order is like his
father's stool.

text: Çukadeva Gosvämé said: In this way, O Mahäräja
sanskrit:
Parékñit, the son named Püru was very pleased to accept the old age
of his father, Yayäti, who took the youth of his son and enjoyed this
material world as he required.

text: Thereafter, King Yayäti became the ruler of the entire
sanskrit:
world, consisting of seven islands, and ruled the citizens exactly like
a father. Because he had taken the youth of his son, his senses were
unimpaired, and he enjoyed as much material happiness as he desired.

text: In secluded places, engaging her mind, words, body and
sanskrit:
various paraphernalia, Devayäné, the dear wife of Mahäräja Yayäti,
always brought her husband the greatest possible transcendental bliss.

text: King Yayäti performed various sacrifices, in which he
sanskrit:
offered abundant gifts to the brähmaëas to satisfy the Supreme Lord,
Hari, who is the reservoir of all the demigods and the object of all
Vedic knowledge.

text: The Supreme Lord, Väsudeva, who created the cosmic
sanskrit:
manifestation, exhibits Himself as all-pervading, like the sky that
holds clouds. And when the creation is annihilated, everything enters
into the Supreme Lord, Viñëu, and varieties are no longer manifested.

text: Without material desires, Mahäräja Yayäti worshiped the
sanskrit:
Supreme Lord, who is situated in everyone's heart as Näräyaëa and is
invisible to material eyes, although existing everywhere.

text: Although Mahäräja Yayäti was the king of the entire
sanskrit:
world and he engaged his mind and five senses in enjoying material
possessions for one thousand years, he was unable to be satisfied.

these three brothers but more qualified, "My dear son, do not be
