sanskrit:
was very much attached to woman. In due course of time, however, when
disgusted with sexual enjoyment and its bad effects, he renounced this
way of life and narrated the following story to his beloved wife.

text: My dearly beloved wife, daughter of Çukräcärya, in this
sanskrit:
world there was someone exactly like me. Please listen as I narrate the
history of his life. By hearing about the life of such a householder,
those who have retired from householder life always lament.

text: While wandering in the forest, eating to satisfy his senses,
sanskrit:
a he-goat by chance approached a well, in which he saw a she-goat
standing helplessly, having fallen into it by the influence of the
results of fruitive activities.

text: After planning how to get the she-goat out of the well, the
sanskrit:
lusty he-goat dug up the earth on the well's edge with the point of his
horns in such a way that she was able to come out very easily.

text: When the she-goat, who had very nice hips, got out of the
sanskrit:
well and saw the very handsome he-goat, she desired to accept him as her
husband. When she did so, many other she-goats also desired him as their
husband because he had a very beautiful bodily structure and a nice
mustache and beard and was expert in discharging semen and in the art of
sexual intercourse. Therefore, just as a person haunted by a ghost
exhibits madness, the best of the he-goats, attracted by the many
she-goats, engaged in erotic activities and naturally forgot his real
business of self-realization.

text: When the she-goat who had fallen into the well saw her
sanskrit:
beloved goat engaged in sexual affairs with another she-goat, she could
not tolerate the goat's activities.

text: Aggrieved by her husband's behavior with another, the
sanskrit:
she-goat thought that the he-goat was not actually her friend but was
hardhearted and was her friend only for the time being. Therefore,
because her husband was lusty, she left him and returned to her former
maintainer.

text: Being very sorry, the he-goat, who was subservient to his
sanskrit:
wife, followed the she-goat on the road and tried his best to flatter
her, but he could not pacify her.

text: The she-goat went to the residence of a brähmaëa who was
sanskrit:
the maintainer of another she-goat, and that brähmaëa angrily cut off
the he-goat's dangling testicles. But at the he-goat's request, the
brähmaëa later rejoined them by the power of mystic yoga.

text: My dear wife, when the he-goat had his testicles restored,
sanskrit:
he enjoyed the she-goat he had gotten from the well, but although he
continued to enjoy for many, many years, even now he has not been fully
satisfied.

text: O my dear wife with beautiful eyebrows, I am exactly like
sanskrit:
that he-goat, for I am so poor in intelligence that I am captivated by
your beauty and have forgotten the real task of self-realization.

text: A person who is lusty cannot satisfy his mind even if he
sanskrit:
has enough of everything in this world, including rice, barley and other
food grains, gold, animals and women. Nothing can satisfy him.

text: As supplying butter to a fire does not diminish the fire
sanskrit:
but instead increases it more and more, the endeavor to stop lusty
desires by continual enjoyment can never be successful. [In fact, one
must voluntarily cease from material desires.]

text: When a man is nonenvious and does not desire ill fortune
sanskrit:
for anyone, he is equipoised. For such a person, all directions appear
happy.

text: For those who are too attached to material enjoyment, sense
sanskrit:
gratification is very difficult to give up. Even when one is an invalid
because of old age, one cannot give up such desires for sense
gratification. Therefore, one who actually desires happiness must give
up such unsatisfied desires, which are the cause of all tribulations.

text: One should not allow oneself to sit on the same seat even
sanskrit:
with one's own mother, sister or daughter, for the senses are so strong
that even though one is very advanced in knowledge, he may be attracted
by sex.

text: I have spent a full one thousand years enjoying sense
sanskrit: gratification, yet my desire to enjoy such pleasure increases daily.

text: Therefore, I shall now give up all these desires and
sanskrit:
meditate upon the Supreme Personality of Godhead. Free from the
dualities of mental concoction and free from false prestige, I shall
wander in the forest with the animals.

text: One who knows that material happiness, whether good or bad,
sanskrit:
in this life or in the next, on this planet or on the heavenly planets,
is temporary and useless, and that an intelligent person should not try
to enjoy or even think of such things, is the knower of the self. Such a
self-realized person knows quite well that material happiness is the
very cause of continued material existence and forgetfulness of one's
own constitutional position.

text: Çukadeva Gosvämé said: After speaking in this way to his
sanskrit:
wife, Devayäné, King Yayäti, who was now free from all material
desires, called his youngest son, Püru, and returned Püru's youth in
exchange for his own old age.

text: King Yayäti gave the southeast to his son Druhyu, the
sanskrit:
south to his son Yadu, the west to his son Turvasu, and the north to his
son Anu. In this way he divided the kingdom.

text: Yayäti enthroned his youngest son, Püru, as the emperor
sanskrit:
of the entire world and the proprietor of all its riches, and he placed
all the other sons, who were older than Püru, under Püru's control.

text: Having enjoyed sense gratification for many, many years, O
sanskrit:
King Parékñit, Yayäti was accustomed to it, but he gave it up
entirely in a moment, just as a bird flies away from the nest as soon as
its wings have grown.

text: Because King Yayäti completely surrendered unto the
sanskrit:
Supreme Personality of Godhead, Väsudeva, he was freed from all
contamination of the material modes of nature. Because of his
self-realization, he was able to fix his mind upon the Transcendence
[Parabrahman, Väsudeva], and thus he ultimately achieved the position
of an associate of the Lord.

sanskrit:
he-goat and she-goat, she understood that this story, which was
presented as if a funny joke for entertainment between husband and wife,
was intended to awaken her to her constitutional position.

sanskrit:
understood that the materialistic association of husband, friends and

text: Çukadeva Gosvämé said: O Mahäräja Parékñit, Yayäti
sanskrit:
was very much attached to woman. In due course of time, however, when
disgusted with sexual enjoyment and its bad effects, he renounced this
way of life and narrated the following story to his beloved wife.

text: My dearly beloved wife, daughter of Çukräcärya, in this
sanskrit:
world there was someone exactly like me. Please listen as I narrate the
history of his life. By hearing about the life of such a householder,
those who have retired from householder life always lament.

text: While wandering in the forest, eating to satisfy his senses,
sanskrit:
a he-goat by chance approached a well, in which he saw a she-goat
standing helplessly, having fallen into it by the influence of the
results of fruitive activities.

text: After planning how to get the she-goat out of the well, the
sanskrit:
lusty he-goat dug up the earth on the well's edge with the point of his
horns in such a way that she was able to come out very easily.

text: When the she-goat, who had very nice hips, got out of the
sanskrit:
well and saw the very handsome he-goat, she desired to accept him as her
husband. When she did so, many other she-goats also desired him as their
husband because he had a very beautiful bodily structure and a nice
mustache and beard and was expert in discharging semen and in the art of
sexual intercourse. Therefore, just as a person haunted by a ghost
exhibits madness, the best of the he-goats, attracted by the many
she-goats, engaged in erotic activities and naturally forgot his real
business of self-realization.

text: When the she-goat who had fallen into the well saw her
sanskrit:
beloved goat engaged in sexual affairs with another she-goat, she could
not tolerate the goat's activities.

text: Aggrieved by her husband's behavior with another, the
sanskrit:
she-goat thought that the he-goat was not actually her friend but was
hardhearted and was her friend only for the time being. Therefore,
because her husband was lusty, she left him and returned to her former
maintainer.

text: Being very sorry, the he-goat, who was subservient to his
sanskrit:
wife, followed the she-goat on the road and tried his best to flatter
her, but he could not pacify her.

text: The she-goat went to the residence of a brähmaëa who was
sanskrit:
the maintainer of another she-goat, and that brähmaëa angrily cut off
the he-goat's dangling testicles. But at the he-goat's request, the
brähmaëa later rejoined them by the power of mystic yoga.

text: My dear wife, when the he-goat had his testicles restored,
sanskrit:
he enjoyed the she-goat he had gotten from the well, but although he
continued to enjoy for many, many years, even now he has not been fully
satisfied.

text: O my dear wife with beautiful eyebrows, I am exactly like
sanskrit:
that he-goat, for I am so poor in intelligence that I am captivated by
your beauty and have forgotten the real task of self-realization.

text: A person who is lusty cannot satisfy his mind even if he
sanskrit:
has enough of everything in this world, including rice, barley and other
food grains, gold, animals and women. Nothing can satisfy him.

text: As supplying butter to a fire does not diminish the fire
sanskrit:
but instead increases it more and more, the endeavor to stop lusty
desires by continual enjoyment can never be successful. [In fact, one
must voluntarily cease from material desires.]

text: When a man is nonenvious and does not desire ill fortune
sanskrit:
for anyone, he is equipoised. For such a person, all directions appear
happy.

text: For those who are too attached to material enjoyment, sense
sanskrit:
gratification is very difficult to give up. Even when one is an invalid
because of old age, one cannot give up such desires for sense
gratification. Therefore, one who actually desires happiness must give
up such unsatisfied desires, which are the cause of all tribulations.

text: One should not allow oneself to sit on the same seat even
sanskrit:
with one's own mother, sister or daughter, for the senses are so strong
that even though one is very advanced in knowledge, he may be attracted
by sex.

text: I have spent a full one thousand years enjoying sense
sanskrit: gratification, yet my desire to enjoy such pleasure increases daily.

text: Therefore, I shall now give up all these desires and
sanskrit:
meditate upon the Supreme Personality of Godhead. Free from the
dualities of mental concoction and free from false prestige, I shall
wander in the forest with the animals.

text: One who knows that material happiness, whether good or bad,
sanskrit:
in this life or in the next, on this planet or on the heavenly planets,
is temporary and useless, and that an intelligent person should not try
to enjoy or even think of such things, is the knower of the self. Such a
self-realized person knows quite well that material happiness is the
very cause of continued material existence and forgetfulness of one's
own constitutional position.

text: Çukadeva Gosvämé said: After speaking in this way to his
sanskrit:
wife, Devayäné, King Yayäti, who was now free from all material
desires, called his youngest son, Püru, and returned Püru's youth in
exchange for his own old age.

text: King Yayäti gave the southeast to his son Druhyu, the
sanskrit:
south to his son Yadu, the west to his son Turvasu, and the north to his
son Anu. In this way he divided the kingdom.

text: Yayäti enthroned his youngest son, Püru, as the emperor
sanskrit:
of the entire world and the proprietor of all its riches, and he placed
all the other sons, who were older than Püru, under Püru's control.

text: Having enjoyed sense gratification for many, many years, O
sanskrit:
King Parékñit, Yayäti was accustomed to it, but he gave it up
entirely in a moment, just as a bird flies away from the nest as soon as
its wings have grown.

text: Because King Yayäti completely surrendered unto the
sanskrit:
Supreme Personality of Godhead, Väsudeva, he was freed from all
contamination of the material modes of nature. Because of his
self-realization, he was able to fix his mind upon the Transcendence
[Parabrahman, Väsudeva], and thus he ultimately achieved the position
of an associate of the Lord.

sanskrit:
he-goat and she-goat, she understood that this story, which was
presented as if a funny joke for entertainment between husband and wife,

text: Çukadeva Gosvämé said: O Mahäräja Parékñit,
sanskrit:
descendant of Mahäräja Bharata, I shall now describe the dynasty of
Püru, in which you were born, in which many saintly kings appeared, and
from which many dynasties of brähmaëas began.

text: King Janamejaya was born of this dynasty of Püru.
sanskrit:
Janamejaya's son was Pracinvän, and his son was Pravéra. Thereafter,
Pravéra's son was Manusyu, and from Manusyu came the son named
Cärupada.

text: The son of Cärupada was Sudyu, and the son of Sudyu was
sanskrit:
Bahugava. Bahugava's son was Saàyäti. From Saàyäti came a son named
Ahaàyäti, from whom Raudräçva was born.

text: Raudräçva had ten sons, named Åteyu, Kakñeyu,
sanskrit:
Sthaëòileyu, Kåteyuka, Jaleyu, Sannateyu, Dharmeyu, Satyeyu, Vrateyu
and Vaneyu. Of these ten sons, Vaneyu was the youngest. As the ten
senses, which are products of the universal life, act under the control
of life, these ten sons of Raudräçva acted under Raudräçva's full
control. All of them were born of the Apsarä named Ghåtäcé.

text: Åteyu had a son named Rantinäva, who had three sons, named
sanskrit:
Sumati, Dhruva and Apratiratha. Apratiratha had only one son, whose name
was Kaëva.

text: The son of Kaëva was Medhätithi, whose sons, all
sanskrit:
brähmaëas, were headed by Praskanna. The son of Rantinäva named
Sumati had a son named Rebhi. Mahäräja Duñmanta is well known as the
son of Rebhi.

text: Once when King Duñmanta went to the forest to hunt and
sanskrit:
was very much fatigued, he approached the residence of Kaëva Muni.
There he saw a most beautiful woman who looked exactly like the goddess
of fortune and who sat there illuminating the entire äçrama by her
effulgence. The King was naturally attracted by her beauty, and
therefore he approached her, accompanied by some of his soldiers, and
spoke to her.

text: Seeing the beautiful woman, the King was very much
sanskrit:
enlivened, and the fatigue of his hunting excursion was relieved. He was
of course very much attracted because of lusty desires, and thus he
inquired from her as follows, in a joking mood.

text: O beautiful lotus-eyed woman, who are you? Whose daughter
sanskrit:
are you? What purpose do you have in this solitary forest? Why are you
staying here?

text: O most beautiful one, it appears to my mind that you must
sanskrit:
be the daughter of a kñatriya. Because I belong to the Püru dynasty,
my mind never endeavors to enjoy anything irreligiously.

text: Çakuntalä said: I am the daughter of Viçvämitra. My
sanskrit:
mother, Menakä, left me in the forest. O hero, the most powerful saint
Kaëva Muni knows all about this. Now let me know, how may I serve you?

text: O King with eyes like the petals of a lotus, kindly come
sanskrit:
sit down and accept whatever reception we can offer. We have a supply of
névärä rice that you may kindly take. And if you so desire, stay here
without hesitation.

text: King Duñmanta replied: O Çakuntalä, with beautiful
sanskrit:
eyebrows, you have taken your birth in the family of the great saint
Viçvämitra, and your reception is quite worthy of your family. Aside
from this, the daughters of a king generally select their own husbands.

text: When Çakuntalä responded to Mahäräja Duñmanta's
sanskrit:
proposal with silence, the agreement was complete. Then the King, who
knew the laws of marriage, immediately married her by chanting the Vedic
praëava [oàkära], in accordance with the marriage ceremony as
performed among the Gandharvas.

text: King Duñmanta, who never discharged semen without a
sanskrit:
result, placed his semen at night in the womb of his Queen, Çakuntalä,
and in the morning he returned to his palace. Thereafter, in due course
of time, Çakuntalä gave birth to a son.

text: In the forest, Kaëva Muni performed all the ritualistic
sanskrit:
ceremonies concerning the newborn child. Later, the boy became so
powerful that he would capture a lion and play with it.

text: Çakuntalä, the best of beautiful women, along with her
sanskrit:
son, whose strength was insurmountable and who was a partial expansion
of the Supreme Godhead, approached her husband, Duñmanta.

text: When the King refused to accept his wife and son, who were
sanskrit:
both irreproachable, an unembodied voice spoke from the sky as an omen
and was heard by everyone present.

text: The voice said: O Mahäräja Duñmanta, a son actually
sanskrit:
belongs to his father, whereas the mother is only a container, like the
skin of a bellows. According to Vedic injunctions, the father is born as
the son. Therefore, maintain your own son and do not insult Çakuntalä.

text: O King Duñmanta, he who discharges semen is the actual
sanskrit:
father, and his son saves him from the custody of Yamaräja. You are the
actual procreator of this child. Indeed, Çakuntalä is speaking the
truth.

text: Çukadeva Gosvämé said: When Mahäräja Duñmanta passed
sanskrit:
away from this earth, his son became the emperor of the world, the
proprietor of the seven islands. He is referred to as a partial
representation of the Supreme Personality of Godhead in this world.

text: Mahäräja Bharata, the son of Duñmanta, had the mark
sanskrit:
of Lord Kåñëa's disc on the palm of his right hand, and he had the
mark of a lotus whorl on the soles of his feet. By worshiping the
Supreme Personality of Godhead with a grand ritualistic ceremony, he
became the emperor and master of the entire world. Then, under the
priesthood of Mämateya, Bhågu Muni, he performed fifty-five horse
sacrifices on the bank of the Ganges, beginning from its mouth and
ending at its source, and seventy-eight horse sacrifices on the bank of
the Yamunä, beginning from the confluence at Prayäga and ending at the
source. He established the sacrificial fire on an excellent site, and he
distributed great wealth to the brähmaëas. Indeed, he distributed so
many cows that each of thousands of brähmaëas had one badva [13,084]
as his share.

text: Bharata, the son of Mahäräja Duñmanta, bound
sanskrit:
thirty-three hundred horses for those sacrifices, and thus he astonished
all other kings. He surpassed even the opulence of the demigods, for he
achieved the supreme spiritual master, Hari.

text: When Mahäräja Bharata performed the sacrifice known as
sanskrit:
Mañëära [or a sacrifice in the place known as Mañëära], he gave in
charity fourteen lakhs of excellent elephants with white tusks and black
bodies, completely covered with golden ornaments.

text: As one cannot approach the heavenly planets simply by the
sanskrit:
strength of his arms (for who can touch the heavenly planets with his
hands?), one cannot imitate the wonderful activities of Mahäräja
Bharata. No one could perform such activities in the past, nor will
anyone be able to do so in the future.

text: When Mahäräja Bharata was on tour, he defeated or killed
sanskrit:
all the Kirätas, Hüëas, Yavanas, Pauëòras, Kaìkas, Khaças, Çakas
and the kings who were opposed to the Vedic principles of brahminical
culture.

text: Formerly, after conquering the demigods, all the demons had
sanskrit:
taken shelter in the lower planetary system known as Rasätala and had
brought all the wives and daughters of the demigods there also.
Mahäräja Bharata, however, rescued all those women, along with their
associates, from the clutches of the demons, and he returned them to the
demigods.

text: Mahäräja Bharata provided all necessities for his
sanskrit:
subjects, both on this earth and in the heavenly planets, for
twenty-seven thousand years. He circulated his orders and distributed
his soldiers in all directions.

text: As the ruler of the entire universe, Emperor Bharata had
sanskrit:
the opulences of a great kingdom and unconquerable soldiers. His sons
and family had seemed to him to be his entire life. But finally he
thought of all this as an impediment to spiritual advancement, and
therefore he ceased from enjoying it.

text: O King Parékñit, Mahäräja Bharata had three pleasing
sanskrit:
wives, who were daughters of the King of Vidarbha. When all three of
them bore children who did not resemble the King, these wives thought
that he would consider them unfaithful queens and reject them, and
therefore they killed their own sons.

text: The King, his attempt for progeny frustrated in this way,
sanskrit:
performed a sacrifice named marut-stoma to get a son. The demigods known
as the Maruts, being fully satisfied with him, then presented him a son
named Bharadväja.

text: When the demigod named Båhaspati was attracted by his
sanskrit:
brother's wife, Mamatä, who at that time was pregnant, he desired to
have sexual relations with her. The son within her womb forbid this, but
Båhaspati cursed him and forcibly discharged semen into the womb of
Mamatä.

text: Mamatä very much feared being forsaken by her husband for
sanskrit:
giving birth to an illegitimate son, and therefore she considered giving
up the child. But then the demigods solved the problem by enunciating a
name for the child.

text: Båhaspati said to Mamatä, "You foolish woman, although
sanskrit:
this child was born from the wife of one man through the semen
discharged by another, you should maintain him." Upon hearing this,
Mamatä replied, "O Båhaspati, you maintain him!" After speaking in
this way, Båhaspati and Mamatä both left. Thus the child was known as
Bharadväja.

text: Although encouraged by the demigods to maintain the child,
sanskrit:
Mamatä considered him useless because of his illicit birth, and
therefore she left him. Consequently, the demigods known as the Maruts
maintained the child, and when Mahäräja Bharata was disappointed for
want of a child, this child was given to him as his son.

sanskrit:
are you? What purpose do you have in this solitary forest? Why are you
staying here?

text: O most beautiful one, it appears to my mind that you must
sanskrit:
be the daughter of a kñatriya. Because I belong to the Püru dynasty,
my mind never endeavors to enjoy anything irreligiously.

text: Çakuntalä said: I am the daughter of Viçvämitra. My
sanskrit:
mother, Menakä, left me in the forest. O hero, the most powerful saint
Kaëva Muni knows all about this. Now let me know, how may I serve you?

text: O King with eyes like the petals of a lotus, kindly come
sanskrit:
sit down and accept whatever reception we can offer. We have a supply of
névärä rice that you may kindly take. And if you so desire, stay here
without hesitation.

text: King Duñmanta replied: O Çakuntalä, with beautiful
sanskrit:
eyebrows, you have taken your birth in the family of the great saint
Viçvämitra, and your reception is quite worthy of your family. Aside
from this, the daughters of a king generally select their own husbands.

text: When Çakuntalä responded to Mahäräja Duñmanta's
sanskrit:
proposal with silence, the agreement was complete. Then the King, who
knew the laws of marriage, immediately married her by chanting the Vedic
praëava [oàkära], in accordance with the marriage ceremony as
performed among the Gandharvas.

text: King Duñmanta, who never discharged semen without a
sanskrit:
result, placed his semen at night in the womb of his Queen, Çakuntalä,
and in the morning he returned to his palace. Thereafter, in due course
of time, Çakuntalä gave birth to a son.

text: In the forest, Kaëva Muni performed all the ritualistic
sanskrit:
ceremonies concerning the newborn child. Later, the boy became so
powerful that he would capture a lion and play with it.

text: Çakuntalä, the best of beautiful women, along with her
sanskrit:
son, whose strength was insurmountable and who was a partial expansion
of the Supreme Godhead, approached her husband, Duñmanta.

text: When the King refused to accept his wife and son, who were
sanskrit:
both irreproachable, an unembodied voice spoke from the sky as an omen
and was heard by everyone present.

text: The voice said: O Mahäräja Duñmanta, a son actually
sanskrit:
belongs to his father, whereas the mother is only a container, like the
skin of a bellows. According to Vedic injunctions, the father is born as
the son. Therefore, maintain your own son and do not insult Çakuntalä.

text: O King Duñmanta, he who discharges semen is the actual
sanskrit:
father, and his son saves him from the custody of Yamaräja. You are the
actual procreator of this child. Indeed, Çakuntalä is speaking the
truth.

text: Çukadeva Gosvämé said: When Mahäräja Duñmanta passed
sanskrit:
away from this earth, his son became the emperor of the world, the
proprietor of the seven islands. He is referred to as a partial
representation of the Supreme Personality of Godhead in this world.

text: Mahäräja Bharata, the son of Duñmanta, had the mark
sanskrit:
of Lord Kåñëa's disc on the palm of his right hand, and he had the
mark of a lotus whorl on the soles of his feet. By worshiping the
Supreme Personality of Godhead with a grand ritualistic ceremony, he
became the emperor and master of the entire world. Then, under the
priesthood of Mämateya, Bhågu Muni, he performed fifty-five horse
sacrifices on the bank of the Ganges, beginning from its mouth and
ending at its source, and seventy-eight horse sacrifices on the bank of
the Yamunä, beginning from the confluence at Prayäga and ending at the
source. He established the sacrificial fire on an excellent site, and he
distributed great wealth to the brähmaëas. Indeed, he distributed so
many cows that each of thousands of brähmaëas had one badva [13,084]
as his share.

text: Bharata, the son of Mahäräja Duñmanta, bound
sanskrit:
thirty-three hundred horses for those sacrifices, and thus he astonished
all other kings. He surpassed even the opulence of the demigods, for he
achieved the supreme spiritual master, Hari.

text: When Mahäräja Bharata performed the sacrifice known as
sanskrit:
Mañëära [or a sacrifice in the place known as Mañëära], he gave in
charity fourteen lakhs of excellent elephants with white tusks and black
bodies, completely covered with golden ornaments.

text: As one cannot approach the heavenly planets simply by the
sanskrit:
strength of his arms (for who can touch the heavenly planets with his
hands?), one cannot imitate the wonderful activities of Mahäräja
Bharata. No one could perform such activities in the past, nor will
anyone be able to do so in the future.

text: When Mahäräja Bharata was on tour, he defeated or killed
sanskrit:
all the Kirätas, Hüëas, Yavanas, Pauëòras, Kaìkas, Khaças, Çakas
and the kings who were opposed to the Vedic principles of brahminical
culture.

text: Formerly, after conquering the demigods, all the demons had
sanskrit:
taken shelter in the lower planetary system known as Rasätala and had
brought all the wives and daughters of the demigods there also.
Mahäräja Bharata, however, rescued all those women, along with their
associates, from the clutches of the demons, and he returned them to the
demigods.

text: Mahäräja Bharata provided all necessities for his
sanskrit:
subjects, both on this earth and in the heavenly planets, for
twenty-seven thousand years. He circulated his orders and distributed
his soldiers in all directions.

text: As the ruler of the entire universe, Emperor Bharata had
sanskrit:
the opulences of a great kingdom and unconquerable soldiers. His sons
and family had seemed to him to be his entire life. But finally he
thought of all this as an impediment to spiritual advancement, and
therefore he ceased from enjoying it.

text: O King Parékñit, Mahäräja Bharata had three pleasing
sanskrit:
wives, who were daughters of the King of Vidarbha. When all three of
them bore children who did not resemble the King, these wives thought
that he would consider them unfaithful queens and reject them, and
therefore they killed their own sons.

text: The King, his attempt for progeny frustrated in this way,
sanskrit:
performed a sacrifice named marut-stoma to get a son. The demigods known
as the Maruts, being fully satisfied with him, then presented him a son
named Bharadväja.

text: When the demigod named Båhaspati was attracted by his
sanskrit:
brother's wife, Mamatä, who at that time was pregnant, he desired to
have sexual relations with her. The son within her womb forbid this, but
Båhaspati cursed him and forcibly discharged semen into the womb of
Mamatä.

text: Mamatä very much feared being forsaken by her husband for
sanskrit:
giving birth to an illegitimate son, and therefore she considered giving
up the child. But then the demigods solved the problem by enunciating a
name for the child.

text: Båhaspati said to Mamatä, "You foolish woman, although
sanskrit:
this child was born from the wife of one man through the semen
discharged by another, you should maintain him." Upon hearing this,
Mamatä replied, "O Båhaspati, you maintain him!" After speaking in
this way, Båhaspati and Mamatä both left. Thus the child was known as
Bharadväja.

text: Although encouraged by the demigods to maintain the child,
sanskrit:
Mamatä considered him useless because of his illicit birth, and
therefore she left him. Consequently, the demigods known as the Maruts
maintained the child, and when Mahäräja Bharata was disappointed for
want of a child, this child was given to him as his son.

text: Çukadeva Gosvämé said: O Mahäräja Parékñit,
sanskrit:
descendant of Mahäräja Bharata, I shall now describe the dynasty of
Püru, in which you were born, in which many saintly kings appeared, and
from which many dynasties of brähmaëas began.

text: King Janamejaya was born of this dynasty of Püru.
sanskrit:
Janamejaya's son was Pracinvän, and his son was Pravéra. Thereafter,
Pravéra's son was Manusyu, and from Manusyu came the son named
Cärupada.

text: The son of Cärupada was Sudyu, and the son of Sudyu was
sanskrit:
Bahugava. Bahugava's son was Saàyäti. From Saàyäti came a son named
Ahaàyäti, from whom Raudräçva was born.

text: Raudräçva had ten sons, named Åteyu, Kakñeyu,
sanskrit:
Sthaëòileyu, Kåteyuka, Jaleyu, Sannateyu, Dharmeyu, Satyeyu, Vrateyu
and Vaneyu. Of these ten sons, Vaneyu was the youngest. As the ten
senses, which are products of the universal life, act under the control
of life, these ten sons of Raudräçva acted under Raudräçva's full
control. All of them were born of the Apsarä named Ghåtäcé.

text: Åteyu had a son named Rantinäva, who had three sons, named
sanskrit:
Sumati, Dhruva and Apratiratha. Apratiratha had only one son, whose name
was Kaëva.

text: The son of Kaëva was Medhätithi, whose sons, all
sanskrit:
brähmaëas, were headed by Praskanna. The son of Rantinäva named
Sumati had a son named Rebhi. Mahäräja Duñmanta is well known as the
son of Rebhi.

text: Once when King Duñmanta went to the forest to hunt and
sanskrit:
was very much fatigued, he approached the residence of Kaëva Muni.
There he saw a most beautiful woman who looked exactly like the goddess
of fortune and who sat there illuminating the entire äçrama by her
effulgence. The King was naturally attracted by her beauty, and
therefore he approached her, accompanied by some of his soldiers, and
spoke to her.

text: Seeing the beautiful woman, the King was very much
sanskrit:
enlivened, and the fatigue of his hunting excursion was relieved. He was
of course very much attracted because of lusty desires, and thus he
inquired from her as follows, in a joking mood.

sanskrit:

text: Çukadeva Gosvämé said: Because Bharadväja was delivered
sanskrit:
by the Marut demigods, he was known as Vitatha. The son of Vitatha was
Manyu, and from Manyu came five sons-Båhatkñatra, Jaya, Mahävérya,
Nara and Garga. Of these five, the one known as Nara had a son named
Saìkåti.

text: O Mahäräja Parékñit, descendant of Päëòu, Saìkåti
sanskrit:
had two sons, named Guru and Rantideva. Rantideva is famous in both this
world and the next, for he is glorified not only in human society but
also in the society of the demigods.

text: Rantideva never endeavored to earn anything. He would
sanskrit:
enjoy whatever he got by the arrangement of providence, but when guests
came he would give them everything. Thus he underwent considerable
suffering, along with the members of his family. Indeed, he and his
family members shivered for want of food and water, yet Rantideva always
remained sober. Once, after fasting for forty-eight days, in the morning
Rantideva received some water and some foodstuffs made with milk and
ghee, but when he and his family were about to eat, a brähmaëa guest
arrived.

text: Because Rantideva perceived the presence of the Supreme
sanskrit:
Godhead everywhere, and in every living entity, he received the guest
with faith and respect and gave him a share of the food. The brähmaëa
guest ate his share and then went away.

text: Thereafter, having divided the remaining food with his
sanskrit:
relatives, Rantideva was just about to eat his own share when a çüdra
guest arrived. Seeing the çüdra in relationship with the Supreme
Personality of Godhead, King Rantideva gave him also a share of the
food.

text: When the çüdra went away, another guest arrived,
sanskrit:
surrounded by dogs, and said, "O King, I and my company of dogs are very
hungry. Please give us something to eat."

text: With great respect, King Rantideva offered the balance of
sanskrit:
the food to the dogs and the master of the dogs, who had come as guests.
The King offered them all respects and obeisances.

text: Thereafter, only the drinking water remained, and there was
sanskrit:
only enough to satisfy one person, but when the King was just about to
drink it, a caëòäla appeared and said, "O King, although I am
lowborn, kindly give me some drinking water."

text: Aggrieved at hearing the pitiable words of the poor
sanskrit:
fatigued caëòäla, Mahäräja Rantideva spoke the following nectarean
words.

text: I do not pray to the Supreme Personality of Godhead for the
sanskrit:
eight perfections of mystic yoga, nor for salvation from repeated birth
and death. I want only to stay among all the living entities and suffer
all distresses on their behalf, so that they may be freed from
suffering.

text: By offering my water to maintain the life of this poor
sanskrit:
caëòäla, who is struggling to live, I have been freed from all
hunger, thirst, fatigue, trembling of the body, moroseness, distress,
lamentation and illusion.

text: Having spoken thus, King Rantideva, although on the verge
sanskrit:
of death because of thirst, gave his own portion of water to the
caëòäla without hesitation, for the King was naturally very kind and
sober.

text: Demigods like Lord Brahmä and Lord Çiva, who can satisfy
sanskrit:
all materially ambitious men by giving them the rewards they desire,
then manifested their own identities before King Rantideva, for it was
they who had presented themselves as the brähmaëa, çüdra, caëòäla
and so on.

text: King Rantideva had no ambition to enjoy material benefits
sanskrit:
from the demigods. He offered them obeisances, but because he was
factually attached to Lord Viñëu, Väsudeva, the Supreme Personality
of Godhead, he fixed his mind at Lord Viñëu's lotus feet.

text: O Mahäräja Parékñit, because King Rantideva was a pure
sanskrit:
devotee, always Kåñëa conscious and free from all material desires,
the Lord's illusory energy, mäyä, could not exhibit herself before
him. On the contrary, for him mäyä entirely vanished, exactly like a
dream.

text: All those who followed the principles of King Rantideva
sanskrit:
were totally favored by his mercy and became pure devotees, attached to
the Supreme Personality of Godhead, Näräyaëa. Thus they all became
the best of yogis.

text: From Garga came a son named Çini, and his son was
sanskrit:
Gärgya. Although Gärgya was a kñatriya, there came from him a
generation of brahmaëas. From Mahävérya came a son named
Duritakñaya, whose sons were Trayyäruëi, Kavi and Puñkaräruëi.
Although these sons of Duritakñaya took birth in a dynasty of
kñatriyas, they too attained the position of brähmaëas. Båhatkñatra
had a son named Hasté, who established the city of Hastinäpura [now
New Delhi].

text: From King Hasté came three sons, named Ajaméòha,
sanskrit:
Dviméòha and Puruméòha. The descendants of Ajaméòha, headed by
Priyamedha, all achieved the position of brähmaëas.

text: From Ajaméòha came a son named Båhadiñu, from
sanskrit:
Båhadiñu came a son named Båhaddhanu, from Båhaddhanu a son named
Båhatkäya, and from Båhatkäya a son named Jayadratha.

text: The son of Jayadratha was Viçada, and his son was
sanskrit:
Syenajit. The sons of Syenajit were Ruciräçva, Dåòhahanu, Käçya
and Vatsa.

text: The son of Ruciräçva was Pära, and the sons of Pära
sanskrit: were Påthusena and Népa. Népa had one hundred sons.

text: King Népa begot a son named Brahmadatta through the womb
sanskrit:
of his wife, Kåtvé, who was the daughter of Çuka. And Brahmadatta,
who was a great yogi, begot a son named Viñvaksena through the womb of
his wife, Sarasvaté.

text: Following the instructions of the great sage Jaigéñavya,
sanskrit:
Viñvaksena compiled an elaborate description of the mystic yoga system.
From Viñvaksena, Udaksena was born, and from Udaksena, Bhalläöa. All
these sons are known as descendants of Båhadiñu.

text: The son of Dviméòha was Yavénara, whose son was
sanskrit:
Kåtimän. The son of Kåtimän was well known as Satyadhåti. From
Satyadhåti came a son named Dåòhanemi, who became the father of
Supärçva.

text: From Supärçva came a son named Sumati, from Sumati
sanskrit:
came Sannatimän, and from Sannatimän came Kåté, who achieved mystic
power from Brahmä and taught six saàhitäs of the Präcyasäma verses
of the Säma Veda. The son of Kåté was Népa; the son of Népa,
Udgräyudha; the son of Udgräyudha, Kñemya; the son of Kñemya,
Suvéra; and the son of Suvéra, Ripuïjaya.

text: From Ripuïjaya came a son named Bahuratha. Puruméòha was
sanskrit:
sonless. Ajaméòha had a son named Néla by his wife known as Naliné,
and the son of Néla was Çänti.

text: The son of Çänti was Suçänti, the son of Suçänti
sanskrit:
was Puruja, and the son of Puruja was Arka. From Arka came Bharmyäçva,
and from Bharmyäçva came five sons-Mudgala, Yavénara, Båhadviçva,
Kämpilla and Saïjaya. Bharmyäçva prayed to his sons, "O my sons,
please take charge of my five states, for you are quite competent to do
so." Thus his five sons were known as the Païcälas. From Mudgala came
a dynasty of brähmaëas known as Maudgalya.

text: Mudgala, the son of Bharmyäçva, had twin children, one
sanskrit:
male and the other female. The male child was named Divodäsa, and the
female child was named Ahalyä. From the womb of Ahalyä by the semen of
her husband, Gautama, came a son named Çatänanda.

text: The son of Çatänanda was Satyadhåti, who was expert in
sanskrit:
archery, and the son of Satyadhåti was Çaradvän. When Çaradvän met
Urvaçé, he discharged semen, which fell on a clump of çara grass.
From this semen were born two all-auspicious babies, one male and the
other female.

text: While Mahäräja Çäntanu was on a hunting excursion, he
sanskrit:
saw the male and female children lying in the forest, and out of
compassion he took them home. Consequently, the male child was known as
Kåpa, and the female child was named Kåpé. Kåpé later became the
wife of Droëäcärya.

text: Çukadeva Gosvämé said: Because Bharadväja was delivered
sanskrit:
by the Marut demigods, he was known as Vitatha. The son of Vitatha was

Nara and Garga. Of these five, the one known as Nara had a son named
Saìkåti.

suffering, along with the members of his family. Indeed, he and his
family members shivered for want of food and water, yet Rantideva always
remained sober. Once, after fasting for forty-eight days, in the morning
Rantideva received some water and some foodstuffs made with milk and
ghee, but when he and his family were about to eat, a brähmaëa guest
arrived.

text: Because Rantideva perceived the presence of the Supreme
sanskrit:
Godhead everywhere, and in every living entity, he received the guest
with faith and respect and gave him a share of the food. The brähmaëa
guest ate his share and then went away.

text: Thereafter, having divided the remaining food with his
sanskrit:
relatives, Rantideva was just about to eat his own share when a çüdra
guest arrived. Seeing the çüdra in relationship with the Supreme
Personality of Godhead, King Rantideva gave him also a share of the
food.

text: When the çüdra went away, another guest arrived,
sanskrit:
surrounded by dogs, and said, "O King, I and my company of dogs are very
hungry. Please give us something to eat."

text: With great respect, King Rantideva offered the balance of
sanskrit:
the food to the dogs and the master of the dogs, who had come as guests.
The King offered them all respects and obeisances.

text: Thereafter, only the drinking water remained, and there was
sanskrit:
only enough to satisfy one person, but when the King was just about to
drink it, a caëòäla appeared and said, "O King, although I am
lowborn, kindly give me some drinking water."

text: Aggrieved at hearing the pitiable words of the poor
sanskrit:
fatigued caëòäla, Mahäräja Rantideva spoke the following nectarean
words.

text: I do not pray to the Supreme Personality of Godhead for the
sanskrit:
eight perfections of mystic yoga, nor for salvation from repeated birth
and death. I want only to stay among all the living entities and suffer
all distresses on their behalf, so that they may be freed from
suffering.

text: By offering my water to maintain the life of this poor
sanskrit:
caëòäla, who is struggling to live, I have been freed from all
hunger, thirst, fatigue, trembling of the body, moroseness, distress,
lamentation and illusion.

text: Having spoken thus, King Rantideva, although on the verge
sanskrit:
of death because of thirst, gave his own portion of water to the
caëòäla without hesitation, for the King was naturally very kind and
sober.

text: Demigods like Lord Brahmä and Lord Çiva, who can satisfy
sanskrit:
all materially ambitious men by giving them the rewards they desire,
then manifested their own identities before King Rantideva, for it was
they who had presented themselves as the brähmaëa, çüdra, caëòäla
and so on.

text: King Rantideva had no ambition to enjoy material benefits
sanskrit:
from the demigods. He offered them obeisances, but because he was
factually attached to Lord Viñëu, Väsudeva, the Supreme Personality
of Godhead, he fixed his mind at Lord Viñëu's lotus feet.

text: O Mahäräja Parékñit, because King Rantideva was a pure
sanskrit:
devotee, always Kåñëa conscious and free from all material desires,
the Lord's illusory energy, mäyä, could not exhibit herself before
him. On the contrary, for him mäyä entirely vanished, exactly like a
dream.

text: All those who followed the principles of King Rantideva
sanskrit:
were totally favored by his mercy and became pure devotees, attached to
the Supreme Personality of Godhead, Näräyaëa. Thus they all became
the best of yogis.

text: From Garga came a son named Çini, and his son was
sanskrit:
Gärgya. Although Gärgya was a kñatriya, there came from him a
generation of brahmaëas. From Mahävérya came a son named
Duritakñaya, whose sons were Trayyäruëi, Kavi and Puñkaräruëi.
Although these sons of Duritakñaya took birth in a dynasty of
kñatriyas, they too attained the position of brähmaëas. Båhatkñatra
had a son named Hasté, who established the city of Hastinäpura [now
New Delhi].

text: From King Hasté came three sons, named Ajaméòha,
sanskrit:
Dviméòha and Puruméòha. The descendants of Ajaméòha, headed by
Priyamedha, all achieved the position of brähmaëas.

text: From Ajaméòha came a son named Båhadiñu, from
sanskrit:
Båhadiñu came a son named Båhaddhanu, from Båhaddhanu a son named
Båhatkäya, and from Båhatkäya a son named Jayadratha.

text: The son of Jayadratha was Viçada, and his son was
sanskrit:
Syenajit. The sons of Syenajit were Ruciräçva, Dåòhahanu, Käçya
and Vatsa.

text: The son of Ruciräçva was Pära, and the sons of Pära
sanskrit: were Påthusena and Népa. Népa had one hundred sons.

text: King Népa begot a son named Brahmadatta through the womb
sanskrit:
of his wife, Kåtvé, who was the daughter of Çuka. And Brahmadatta,
who was a great yogi, begot a son named Viñvaksena through the womb of
his wife, Sarasvaté.

text: Following the instructions of the great sage Jaigéñavya,
sanskrit:
Viñvaksena compiled an elaborate description of the mystic yoga system.
From Viñvaksena, Udaksena was born, and from Udaksena, Bhalläöa. All
these sons are known as descendants of Båhadiñu.

text: The son of Dviméòha was Yavénara, whose son was
sanskrit:
Kåtimän. The son of Kåtimän was well known as Satyadhåti. From
Satyadhåti came a son named Dåòhanemi, who became the father of
Supärçva.

text: From Supärçva came a son named Sumati, from Sumati
sanskrit:
came Sannatimän, and from Sannatimän came Kåté, who achieved mystic
power from Brahmä and taught six saàhitäs of the Präcyasäma verses
of the Säma Veda. The son of Kåté was Népa; the son of Népa,
Udgräyudha; the son of Udgräyudha, Kñemya; the son of Kñemya,
Suvéra; and the son of Suvéra, Ripuïjaya.

text: From Ripuïjaya came a son named Bahuratha. Puruméòha was
sanskrit:
sonless. Ajaméòha had a son named Néla by his wife known as Naliné,
and the son of Néla was Çänti.

text: The son of Çänti was Suçänti, the son of Suçänti
sanskrit:
was Puruja, and the son of Puruja was Arka. From Arka came Bharmyäçva,
and from Bharmyäçva came five sons-Mudgala, Yavénara, Båhadviçva,
Kämpilla and Saïjaya. Bharmyäçva prayed to his sons, "O my sons,
please take charge of my five states, for you are quite competent to do
so." Thus his five sons were known as the Païcälas. From Mudgala came
a dynasty of brähmaëas known as Maudgalya.

text: Mudgala, the son of Bharmyäçva, had twin children, one
sanskrit:
male and the other female. The male child was named Divodäsa, and the
female child was named Ahalyä. From the womb of Ahalyä by the semen of
her husband, Gautama, came a son named Çatänanda.

text: The son of Çatänanda was Satyadhåti, who was expert in
sanskrit:
archery, and the son of Satyadhåti was Çaradvän. When Çaradvän met
Urvaçé, he discharged semen, which fell on a clump of çara grass.
From this semen were born two all-auspicious babies, one male and the
other female.

text: While Mahäräja Çäntanu was on a hunting excursion, he
sanskrit:
saw the male and female children lying in the forest, and out of
compassion he took them home. Consequently, the male child was known as
Kåpa, and the female child was named Kåpé. Kåpé later became the
wife of Droëäcärya.

text: Çukadeva Gosvämé said: Because Bharadväja was delivered
sanskrit:
by the Marut demigods, he was known as Vitatha. The son of Vitatha was
Manyu, and from Manyu came five sons-Båhatkñatra, Jaya, Mahävérya,
Nara and Garga. Of these five, the one known as Nara had a son named
Saìkåti.

text: O Mahäräja Parékñit, descendant of Päëòu, Saìkåti
sanskrit:
had two sons, named Guru and Rantideva. Rantideva is famous in both this
world and the next, for he is glorified not only in human society but
also in the society of the demigods.

text: Rantideva never endeavored to earn anything. He would
sanskrit:
enjoy whatever he got by the arrangement of providence, but when guests
came he would give them everything. Thus he underwent considerable
suffering, along with the members of his family. Indeed, he and his
family members shivered for want of food and water, yet Rantideva always
remained sober. Once, after fasting for forty-eight days, in the morning
Rantideva received some water and some foodstuffs made with milk and
ghee, but when he and his family were about to eat, a brähmaëa guest
arrived.

text: Because Rantideva perceived the presence of the Supreme
sanskrit:
Godhead everywhere, and in every living entity, he received the guest

guest ate his share and then went away.

text: Thereafter, having divided the remaining food with his
sanskrit:

text: With great respect, King Rantideva offered the balance of
sanskrit:
the food to the dogs and the master of the dogs, who had come as guests.
The King offered them all respects and obeisances.

sanskrit:

text: From Ajaméòha came a son named Båhadiñu, from
sanskrit:
Båhadiñu came a son named Båhaddhanu, from Båhaddhanu a son named
Båhatkäya, and from Båhatkäya a son named Jayadratha.

text: The son of Jayadratha was Viçada, and his son was
sanskrit:
Syenajit. The sons of Syenajit were Ruciräçva, Dåòhahanu, Käçya
and Vatsa.

text: The son of Ruciräçva was Pära, and the sons of Pära
sanskrit: were Påthusena and Népa. Népa had one hundred sons.

text: King Népa begot a son named Brahmadatta through the womb
sanskrit:

sanskrit:

sanskrit:

text: From Supärçva came a son named Sumati, from Sumati
sanskrit:

Suvéra; and the son of Suvéra, Ripuïjaya.

text: From Ripuïjaya came a son named Bahuratha. Puruméòha was
sanskrit:
sonless. Ajaméòha had a son named Néla by his wife known as Naliné,
and the son of Néla was Çänti.

text: The son of Çänti was Suçänti, the son of Suçänti
sanskrit:
was Puruja, and the son of Puruja was Arka. From Arka came Bharmyäçva,
and from Bharmyäçva came five sons-Mudgala, Yavénara, Båhadviçva,
Kämpilla and Saïjaya. Bharmyäçva prayed to his sons, "O my sons,
please take charge of my five states, for you are quite competent to do

text: Mudgala, the son of Bharmyäçva, had twin children, one
sanskrit:
male and the other female. The male child was named Divodäsa, and the
female child was named Ahalyä. From the womb of Ahalyä by the semen of

text: The son of Çatänanda was Satyadhåti, who was expert in
sanskrit:
archery, and the son of Satyadhåti was Çaradvän. When Çaradvän met
Urvaçé, he discharged semen, which fell on a clump of çara grass.
From this semen were born two all-auspicious babies, one male and the

sanskrit:
saw the male and female children lying in the forest, and out of
compassion he took them home. Consequently, the male child was known as
Kåpa, and the female child was named Kåpé. Kåpé later became the
wife of Droëäcärya.

text: Çukadeva Gosvämé said: O King, the son of Divodäsa was
sanskrit:
Miträyu, and from Miträyu came four sons, named Cyavana, Sudäsa,
Sahadeva and Somaka. Somaka was the father of Jantu.

text: Somaka had one hundred sons, of whom the youngest was
sanskrit:
Påñata. From Påñata was born King Drupada, who was opulent in all
supremacy.

text: From Mahäräja Drupada, Draupadé was born. Mahäräja
sanskrit:
Drupada also had many sons, headed by Dhåñöadyumna. From
Dhåñöadyumna came a son named Dhåñöaketu. All these personalities
are known as descendants of Bharmyäçva or as the dynasty of
Päïcäla.

text: Another son of Ajaméòha was known as Åkña. From Åkña
sanskrit:
came a son named Saàvaraëa, and from Saàvaraëa through the womb of
his wife, Tapaté, the daughter of the sun-god, came Kuru, the King of
Kurukñetra. Kuru had four sons-Parékñi, Sudhanu, Jahnu and Niñadha.
From Sudhanu, Suhotra was born, and from Suhotra, Cyavana. From Cyavana,
Kåté was born.

text: The son of Kåté was Uparicara Vasu, and among his sons,
sanskrit:
headed by Båhadratha, were Kuçämba, Matsya, Pratyagra and Cedipa. All
the sons of Uparicara Vasu became rulers of the Cedi state.

text: From Båhadratha, Kuçägra was born; from Kuçägra,
sanskrit:
Åñabha; and from Åñabha, Satyahita. The son of Satyahita was
Puñpavän, and the son of Puñpavän was Jahu.

text: Through the womb of another wife, Båhadratha begot two
sanskrit:
halves of a son. When the mother saw those two halves she rejected them,
but later a she-demon named Jarä playfully joined them and said, "Come
to life, come to life!" Thus the son named Jaräsandha was born.

text: From Jaräsandha came a son named Sahadeva; from Sahadeva,
sanskrit:
Somäpi; and from Somäpi, Çrutaçravä. The son of Kuru called
Parékñi had no sons, but the son of Kuru called Jahnu had a son named
Suratha.

text: From Suratha came a son named Vidüratha, from whom
sanskrit:
Särvabhauma was born. From Särvabhauma came Jayasena; from Jayasena,
Rädhika; and from Rädhika, Ayutäyu.

text: From Ayutäyu came a son named Akrodhana, and his son was
sanskrit:
Devätithi. The son of Devätithi was Åkña, the son of Åkña was
Dilépa, and the son of Dilépa was Pratépa.

text: The sons of Pratépa were Deväpi, Çäntanu and
sanskrit:
Bähléka. Deväpi left the kingdom of his father and went to the
forest, and therefore Çäntanu became the king. Çäntanu, who in his
previous birth was known as Mahäbhiña, had the ability to transform
anyone from old age to youth simply by touching that person with his
hands.

text: Because the King was able to make everyone happy for
sanskrit:
sense gratification, primarily by the touch of his hand, his name was
Çäntanu. Once, when there was no rainfall in the kingdom for twelve
years and the King consulted his learned brahminical advisors, they
said, "You are faulty for enjoying the property of your elder brother.
For the elevation of your kingdom and home, you should return the
kingdom to him."

text: When the brähmaëas said this, Mahäräja Çäntanu
sanskrit:
went to the forest and requested his elder brother Deväpi to take
charge of the kingdom, for it is the duty of a king to maintain his
subjects. Previously, however, Çäntanu's minister Açvavära had
instigated some brähmaëas to induce Deväpi to transgress the
injunctions of the Vedas and thus make himself unfit for the post of
ruler. The brähmaëas deviated Deväpi from the path of the Vedic
principles, and therefore when asked by Çäntanu he did not agree to
accept the post of ruler. On the contrary, he blasphemed the Vedic
principles and therefore became fallen. Under the circumstances,
Çäntanu again became the king, and Indra, being pleased, showered
rains. Deväpi later took to the path of mystic yoga to control his mind
and senses and went to the village named Kaläpagräma, where he is
still living.

text: After the dynasty of the moon-god comes to an end in
sanskrit:
this age of Kali, Deväpi, in the beginning of the next Satya-yuga, will
reestablish the Soma dynasty in this world. From Bähléka [the brother
of Çäntanu] came a son named Somadatta, who had three sons, named
Bhüri, Bhüriçravä and Çala. From Çäntanu, through the womb of his
wife named Gaìgä, came Bhéñma, the exalted, self-realized devotee
and learned scholar.

text: Bhéñmadeva was the foremost of all warriors. When he
sanskrit:
defeated Lord Paraçuräma in a fight, Lord Paraçuräma was very
satisfied with him. By the semen of Çäntanu in the womb of Satyavaté,
the daughter of a fisherman, Citräìgada took birth.

text: Citräìgada, of whom Vicitravérya was the younger
sanskrit:
brother, was killed by a Gandharva who was also named Citräìgada.
Satyavaté, before her marriage to Çäntanu, gave birth to the master
authority of the Vedas, Vyäsadeva, known as Kåñëa Dvaipäyana, who
was begotten by Paräçara Muni. From Vyäsadeva, I [Çukadeva
Gosvämé] was born, and from him I studied this great work of
literature, Çrémad-Bhägavatam. The incarnation of Godhead Vedavyäsa,
rejecting his disciples, headed by Paila, instructed
Çrémad-Bhägavatam to me because I was free from all material desires.
After Ambikä and Ambälikä, the two daughters of Käçéräja, were
taken away by force, Vicitravérya married them, but because he was too
attached to these two wives, he had a heart attack and died of
tuberculosis.

text: Bädaräyaëa, Çré Vyäsadeva, following the order of his
sanskrit:
mother, Satyavaté, begot three sons, two by the womb of Ambikä and
Ambälikä, the two wives of his brother Vicitravérya, and the third by
Vicitravérya's maidservant. These sons were Dhåtaräñöra, Päëòu
and Vidura.

text: Dhåtaräñöra's wife, Gändhäré, gave birth to one
sanskrit:
hundred sons and one daughter, O King. The oldest of the sons was
Duryodhana, and the daughter's name was Duùçalä.

text: Päëòu was restrained from sexual life because of
sanskrit:
having been cursed by a sage, and therefore his three sons
Yudhiñöhira, Bhéma and Arjuna were begotten through the womb of his
wife, Kunté, by Dharmaräja, by the demigod controlling the wind, and
by the demigod controlling the rain. Päëòu's second wife, Mädré,
gave birth to Nakula and Sahadeva, who were begotten by the two
Açviné-kumäras. The five brothers, headed by Yudhiñöhira, begot
five sons through the womb of Draupadé. These five sons were your
uncles.

text: From Yudhiñöhira came a son named Prativindhya, from
sanskrit:
Bhéma a son named Çrutasena, from Arjuna a son named Çrutakérti, and
from Nakula a son named Çatänéka.

text: O King, the son of Sahadeva was Çrutakarmä.
sanskrit:
Furthermore, Yudhiñöhira and his brothers begot other sons in other
wives. Yudhiñöhira begot a son named Devaka through the womb of
Pauravé, and Bhémasena begot a son named Ghaöotkaca through his wife
Hiòimbä and a son named Sarvagata through his wife Kälé. Similarly,
Sahadeva had a son named Suhotra through his wife named Vijayä, who was
the daughter of the king of the mountains.

text: Nakula begot a son named Naramitra through his wife named
sanskrit:
Kareëumaté. Similarly, Arjuna begot a son named Irävän through his
wife known as Ulupé, the daughter of the Nägas, and a son named
Babhruvähana by the womb of the princess of Maëipura. Babhruvähana
became the adopted son of the king of Maëipura.

text: My dear King Parékñit, your father, Abhimanyu, was born
sanskrit:
from the womb of Subhadrä as the son of Arjuna. He was the conqueror of
all atirathas [those who could fight with one thousand charioteers].
From him, by the womb of Uttarä, the daughter of Viräòräja, you were
born.

text: After the Kuru dynasty was annihilated in the Battle of
sanskrit:
Kurukñetra, you also were about to be destroyed by the brahmästra
atomic weapon released by the son of Droëäcärya, but by the mercy of
the Supreme Personality of Godhead, Kåñëa, you were saved from death.

text: My dear King, your four sons-Janamejaya, Çrutasena,
sanskrit: Bhémasena and Ugrasena-are very powerful. Janamejaya is the eldest.

text: Because of your death by the Takñaka snake, your son
sanskrit:
Janamejaya will be very angry and will perform a sacrifice to kill all
the snakes in the world.

text: After conquering throughout the world and after accepting
sanskrit:
Tura, the son of Kalaña, as his priest, Janamejaya will perform
açvamedha-yajïas, for which he will be known as Turaga-medhañäö.

text: The son of Janamejaya known as Çatänéka will learn from
sanskrit:
Yäjïavalkya the three Vedas and the art of performing ritualistic
ceremonies. He will also learn the military art from Kåpäcärya and
the transcendental science from the sage Çaunaka.

text: The son of Çatänéka will be Sahasränéka, and from him
sanskrit:
will come the son named Açvamedhaja. From Açvamedhaja will come
Asémakåñëa, and his son will be Nemicakra.

text: When the town of Hastinäpura [New Delhi] is inundated by
sanskrit:
the river, Nemicakra will live in the place known as Kauçämbé. His
son will be celebrated as Citraratha, and the son of Citraratha will be
Çuciratha.

text: From Çuciratha will come the son named Våñöimän, and
sanskrit:
his son, Suñeëa, will be the emperor of the entire world. The son of

will come a son named Sukhénala.

text: The son of Sukhénala will be Pariplava, and his son will
sanskrit:
be Sunaya. From Sunaya will come a son named Medhävé; from Medhävé,
Nåpaïjaya; from Nåpaïjaya, Dürva; and from Dürva, Timi.

text: From Timi will come Båhadratha; from Båhadratha, Sudäsa;
sanskrit:
and from Sudäsa, Çatänéka. From Çatänéka will come Durdamana, and
from him will come a son named Mahénara.

text: The son of Mahénara will be Daëòapäëi, and his son
sanskrit:
will be Nimi, from whom King Kñemaka will be born. I have now described
to you the moon-god's dynasty, which is the source of brähmaëas and
kñatriyas and is worshiped by demigods and great saints. In this
Kali-yuga, Kñemaka will be the last monarch. Now I shall describe to
you the future of the Mägadha dynasty. Please listen.

text: Sahadeva, the son of Jaräsandha, will have a son named
sanskrit:
Märjäri. From Märjäri will come Çrutaçravä; from Çrutaçravä,
Yutäyu; and from Yutäyu, Niramitra. The son of Niramitra will be
Sunakñatra, from Sunakñatra will come Båhatsena, and from Båhatsena,
Karmajit. The son of Karmajit will be Sutaïjaya, the son of Sutaïjaya
will be Vipra, and his son will be Çuci. The son of Çuci will be
Kñema, the son of Kñema will be Suvrata, and the son of Suvrata will
be Dharmasütra. From Dharmasütra will come Sama; from Sama,
Dyumatsena; from Dyumatsena, Sumati; and from Sumati, Subala.

text: From Subala will come Sunétha; from Sunétha, Satyajit;
sanskrit:
from Satyajit, Viçvajit; and from Viçvajit, Ripuïjaya. All of these
personalities will belong to the dynasty of Båhadratha, which will rule
the world for one thousand years.

text: Çukadeva Gosvämé said: O King, the son of Divodäsa was
sanskrit:
Miträyu, and from Miträyu came four sons, named Cyavana, Sudäsa,
Sahadeva and Somaka. Somaka was the father of Jantu.

text: Somaka had one hundred sons, of whom the youngest was
sanskrit:
Påñata. From Påñata was born King Drupada, who was opulent in all
supremacy.

text: From Mahäräja Drupada, Draupadé was born. Mahäräja
sanskrit:
Drupada also had many sons, headed by Dhåñöadyumna. From
Dhåñöadyumna came a son named Dhåñöaketu. All these personalities
are known as descendants of Bharmyäçva or as the dynasty of
Päïcäla.

text: Another son of Ajaméòha was known as Åkña. From Åkña
sanskrit:
came a son named Saàvaraëa, and from Saàvaraëa through the womb of
his wife, Tapaté, the daughter of the sun-god, came Kuru, the King of
Kurukñetra. Kuru had four sons-Parékñi, Sudhanu, Jahnu and Niñadha.
From Sudhanu, Suhotra was born, and from Suhotra, Cyavana. From Cyavana,
Kåté was born.

text: The son of Kåté was Uparicara Vasu, and among his sons,
sanskrit:
headed by Båhadratha, were Kuçämba, Matsya, Pratyagra and Cedipa. All
the sons of Uparicara Vasu became rulers of the Cedi state.

text: From Båhadratha, Kuçägra was born; from Kuçägra,
sanskrit:
Åñabha; and from Åñabha, Satyahita. The son of Satyahita was
Puñpavän, and the son of Puñpavän was Jahu.

text: Through the womb of another wife, Båhadratha begot two
sanskrit:
halves of a son. When the mother saw those two halves she rejected them,
but later a she-demon named Jarä playfully joined them and said, "Come
to life, come to life!" Thus the son named Jaräsandha was born.

text: From Jaräsandha came a son named Sahadeva; from Sahadeva,
sanskrit:
Somäpi; and from Somäpi, Çrutaçravä. The son of Kuru called
Parékñi had no sons, but the son of Kuru called Jahnu had a son named
Suratha.

text: From Suratha came a son named Vidüratha, from whom
sanskrit:
Särvabhauma was born. From Särvabhauma came Jayasena; from Jayasena,
Rädhika; and from Rädhika, Ayutäyu.

text: From Ayutäyu came a son named Akrodhana, and his son was
sanskrit:
Devätithi. The son of Devätithi was Åkña, the son of Åkña was
Dilépa, and the son of Dilépa was Pratépa.

text: The sons of Pratépa were Deväpi, Çäntanu and
sanskrit:
Bähléka. Deväpi left the kingdom of his father and went to the
forest, and therefore Çäntanu became the king. Çäntanu, who in his
previous birth was known as Mahäbhiña, had the ability to transform
anyone from old age to youth simply by touching that person with his
hands.

text: Because the King was able to make everyone happy for
sanskrit:
sense gratification, primarily by the touch of his hand, his name was
Çäntanu. Once, when there was no rainfall in the kingdom for twelve
years and the King consulted his learned brahminical advisors, they
said, "You are faulty for enjoying the property of your elder brother.
For the elevation of your kingdom and home, you should return the
kingdom to him."

text: When the brähmaëas said this, Mahäräja Çäntanu
sanskrit:
went to the forest and requested his elder brother Deväpi to take
charge of the kingdom, for it is the duty of a king to maintain his
subjects. Previously, however, Çäntanu's minister Açvavära had
instigated some brähmaëas to induce Deväpi to transgress the
injunctions of the Vedas and thus make himself unfit for the post of
ruler. The brähmaëas deviated Deväpi from the path of the Vedic
principles, and therefore when asked by Çäntanu he did not agree to
accept the post of ruler. On the contrary, he blasphemed the Vedic
principles and therefore became fallen. Under the circumstances,
Çäntanu again became the king, and Indra, being pleased, showered
rains. Deväpi later took to the path of mystic yoga to control his mind
and senses and went to the village named Kaläpagräma, where he is
still living.

text: After the dynasty of the moon-god comes to an end in
sanskrit:
this age of Kali, Deväpi, in the beginning of the next Satya-yuga, will
reestablish the Soma dynasty in this world. From Bähléka [the brother
of Çäntanu] came a son named Somadatta, who had three sons, named
Bhüri, Bhüriçravä and Çala. From Çäntanu, through the womb of his
wife named Gaìgä, came Bhéñma, the exalted, self-realized devotee
and learned scholar.

text: Bhéñmadeva was the foremost of all warriors. When he
sanskrit:
defeated Lord Paraçuräma in a fight, Lord Paraçuräma was very
satisfied with him. By the semen of Çäntanu in the womb of Satyavaté,
the daughter of a fisherman, Citräìgada took birth.

text: Citräìgada, of whom Vicitravérya was the younger
sanskrit:
brother, was killed by a Gandharva who was also named Citräìgada.
Satyavaté, before her marriage to Çäntanu, gave birth to the master
authority of the Vedas, Vyäsadeva, known as Kåñëa Dvaipäyana, who
was begotten by Paräçara Muni. From Vyäsadeva, I [Çukadeva
Gosvämé] was born, and from him I studied this great work of
literature, Çrémad-Bhägavatam. The incarnation of Godhead Vedavyäsa,
rejecting his disciples, headed by Paila, instructed
Çrémad-Bhägavatam to me because I was free from all material desires.
After Ambikä and Ambälikä, the two daughters of Käçéräja, were
taken away by force, Vicitravérya married them, but because he was too
attached to these two wives, he had a heart attack and died of
tuberculosis.

text: Bädaräyaëa, Çré Vyäsadeva, following the order of his
sanskrit:
mother, Satyavaté, begot three sons, two by the womb of Ambikä and
Ambälikä, the two wives of his brother Vicitravérya, and the third by
Vicitravérya's maidservant. These sons were Dhåtaräñöra, Päëòu
and Vidura.

text: Dhåtaräñöra's wife, Gändhäré, gave birth to one
sanskrit:
hundred sons and one daughter, O King. The oldest of the sons was
Duryodhana, and the daughter's name was Duùçalä.

text: Päëòu was restrained from sexual life because of
sanskrit:
having been cursed by a sage, and therefore his three sons
Yudhiñöhira, Bhéma and Arjuna were begotten through the womb of his
wife, Kunté, by Dharmaräja, by the demigod controlling the wind, and
by the demigod controlling the rain. Päëòu's second wife, Mädré,
gave birth to Nakula and Sahadeva, who were begotten by the two
Açviné-kumäras. The five brothers, headed by Yudhiñöhira, begot
five sons through the womb of Draupadé. These five sons were your
uncles.

text: From Yudhiñöhira came a son named Prativindhya, from
sanskrit:
Bhéma a son named Çrutasena, from Arjuna a son named Çrutakérti, and
from Nakula a son named Çatänéka.

text: O King, the son of Sahadeva was Çrutakarmä.
sanskrit:
Furthermore, Yudhiñöhira and his brothers begot other sons in other
wives. Yudhiñöhira begot a son named Devaka through the womb of

Hiòimbä and a son named Sarvagata through his wife Kälé. Similarly,
Sahadeva had a son named Suhotra through his wife named Vijayä, who was
the daughter of the king of the mountains.

text: Nakula begot a son named Naramitra through his wife named
sanskrit:
Kareëumaté. Similarly, Arjuna begot a son named Irävän through his
wife known as Ulupé, the daughter of the Nägas, and a son named

became the adopted son of the king of Maëipura.

text: My dear King Parékñit, your father, Abhimanyu, was born
sanskrit:
from the womb of Subhadrä as the son of Arjuna. He was the conqueror of
all atirathas [those who could fight with one thousand charioteers].

born.

sanskrit:

sanskrit: Bhémasena and Ugrasena-are very powerful. Janamejaya is the eldest.

sanskrit:

sanskrit:

sanskrit:

will be Nimi, from whom King Kñemaka will be born. I have now described
to you the moon-god's dynasty, which is the source of brähmaëas and
kñatriyas and is worshiped by demigods and great saints. In this
Kali-yuga, Kñemaka will be the last monarch. Now I shall describe to
you the future of the Mägadha dynasty. Please listen.

text: Sahadeva, the son of Jaräsandha, will have a son named
sanskrit:
Märjäri. From Märjäri will come Çrutaçravä; from Çrutaçravä,
Yutäyu; and from Yutäyu, Niramitra. The son of Niramitra will be
Sunakñatra, from Sunakñatra will come Båhatsena, and from Båhatsena,
Karmajit. The son of Karmajit will be Sutaïjaya, the son of Sutaïjaya
will be Vipra, and his son will be Çuci. The son of Çuci will be
Kñema, the son of Kñema will be Suvrata, and the son of Suvrata will
be Dharmasütra. From Dharmasütra will come Sama; from Sama,
Dyumatsena; from Dyumatsena, Sumati; and from Sumati, Subala.

text: From Subala will come Sunétha; from Sunétha, Satyajit;
sanskrit:
from Satyajit, Viçvajit; and from Viçvajit, Ripuïjaya. All of these
personalities will belong to the dynasty of Båhadratha, which will rule
the world for one thousand years.

text: Çukadeva Gosvämé said: Anu, the fourth son of Yayäti,
sanskrit:
had three sons, named Sabhänara, Cakñu and Pareñëu. O King, from
Sabhänara came a son named Kälanara, and from Kälanara came a son
named Såïjaya.

text: From Såïjaya came a son named Janamejaya. From Janamejaya
sanskrit:
came Mahäçäla; from Mahäçäla, Mahämanä; and from Mahämanä two
sons, named Uçénara and Titikñu.

text: The four sons of Uçénara were Çibi, Vara, Kåmi and
sanskrit:
Dakña, and from Çibi again came four sons, named Våñädarbha,
Sudhéra, Madra and ätma-tattva-vit Kekaya. The son of Titikñu was
Ruñadratha. From Ruñadratha came Homa; from Homa, Sutapä; and from
Sutapä, Bali.

text: By the semen of Dérghatama in the wife of Bali, the emperor
sanskrit:
of the world, six sons took birth, namely Aìga, Vaìga, Kaliìga,
Suhma, Puëòra and Oòra.

text: These six sons, headed by Aìga, later became kings of six
sanskrit:
states in the eastern side of India. These states were known according
to the names of their respective kings. From Aìga came a son named
Khalapäna, and from Khalapäna came Diviratha.

text: From Diviratha came a son named Dharmaratha, and his son
sanskrit:
was Citraratha, who was celebrated as Romapäda. Romapäda, however, was
without issue, and therefore his friend Mahäräja Daçaratha gave him
his own daughter, named Çäntä. Romapäda accepted her as his
daughter, and thereafter she married Åñyaçåìga. When the demigods
from the heavenly planets failed to shower rain, Åñyaçåìga was
appointed the priest for performing a sacrifice, after being brought
from the forest by the allurement of prostitutes, who danced, staged
theatrical performances accompanied by music, and embraced and worshiped
him. After Åñyaçåìga came, the rain fell. Thereafter,
Åñyaçåìga performed a son-giving sacrifice on behalf of Mahäräja
Daçaratha, who had no issue, and then Mahäräja Daçaratha had sons.
From Romapäda, by the mercy of Åñyaçåìga, Caturaìga was born, and
from Caturaìga came Påthuläkña.

text: The sons of Påthuläkña were Båhadratha, Båhatkarmä
sanskrit:
and Båhadbhänu. From the eldest, Båhadratha, came a son named
Båhanmanä, and from Båhanmanä came a son named Jayadratha.

text: The son of Jayadratha, by the womb of his wife Sambhüti,
sanskrit:
was Vijaya, and from Vijaya, Dhåti was born. From Dhåti came
Dhåtavrata; from Dhåtavrata, Satkarmä; and from Satkarmä, Adhiratha.

text: While playing on the bank of the Ganges, Adhiratha found a
sanskrit:
baby wrapped up in a basket. The baby had been left by Kunté because he
was born before she was married. Because Adhiratha had no sons, he
raised this baby as his own. [This son was later known as Karëa.]

text: O King, the only son of Karëa was Våñasena. Druhyu, the
sanskrit:
third son of Yayäti, had a son named Babhru, and the son of Babhru was
known as Setu.

text: The son of Setu was Ärabdha, Ärabdha's son was
sanskrit:
Gändhära, and Gändhära's son was Dharma. Dharma's son was Dhåta,
Dhåta's son was Durmada, and Durmada's son was Pracetä, who had one
hundred sons.

text: The Pracetäs [the sons of Pracetä] occupied the northern
The son of Bhänumän was Tribhänu, and his son was the
sanskrit:
magnanimous Karandhama. Karandhama's son was Maruta, who had no sons and
who therefore adopted a son of the Püru dynasty [Mahäräja Duñmanta]
as his own.

text: Mahäräja Duñmanta, desiring to occupy the throne,
sanskrit:
returned to his original dynasty [the Püru dynasty], even though he had
accepted Maruta as his father. O Mahäräja Parékñit, let me now
describe the dynasty of Yadu, the eldest son of Mahäräja Yayäti. This
description is supremely pious, and it vanquishes the reactions of
sinful activities in human society. Simply by hearing this description,
one is freed from all sinful reactions.

text: The Supreme Personality of Godhead, Kåñëa, the
sanskrit:
Supersoul in the hearts of all living entities, descended in His
original form as a human being in the dynasty or family of Yadu. Yadu
had four sons, named Sahasrajit, Kroñöä, Nala and Ripu. Of these
four, the eldest, Sahasrajit, had a son named Çatajit, who had three
sons, named Mahähaya, Reëuhaya and Haihaya.

text: The son of Haihaya was Dharma, and the son of Dharma was
sanskrit:
Netra, the father of Kunti. From Kunti came a son named Sohaïji, from
Sohaïji came Mahiñmän, and from Mahiñmän, Bhadrasenaka.

text: The sons of Bhadrasena were known as Durmada and Dhanaka.
sanskrit:
Dhanaka was the father of Kåtavérya and also of Kåtägni, Kåtavarmä
and Kåtaujä.

text: The son of Kåtavérya was Arjuna. He [Kärtavéryärjuna]
sanskrit:
became the emperor of the entire world, consisting of seven islands, and
received mystic power from Dattätreya, the incarnation of the Supreme
Personality of Godhead. Thus he obtained the mystic perfections known as
asta-siddhi.

text: No other king in this world could equal Kärtavéryärjuna
sanskrit:
in sacrifices, charity, austerity, mystic power, education, strength or
mercy.

text: For eighty-five thousand years, Kärtavéryärjuna
sanskrit:
continuously enjoyed material opulences with full bodily strength and
unimpaired memory. In other words, he enjoyed inexhaustible material
opulences with his six senses.

text: Of the one thousand sons of Kärtavéryärjuna, only five
sanskrit:
remained alive after the fight with Paraçuräma. Their names were
Jayadhvaja, Çürasena, Våñabha, Madhu and Ürjita.

text: Jayadhvaja had a son named Tälajaìgha, who had one
sanskrit:
hundred sons. All the kñatriyas in that dynasty, known as Tälajaìgha,
were annihilated by the great power received by Mahäräja Sagara from
Aurva Åñi.

text: Of the sons of Tälajaìgha, Vétihotra was the eldest. The
sanskrit:
son of Vétihotra named Madhu had a celebrated son named Våñëi. Madhu
had one hundred sons, of whom Våñëi was the eldest. The dynasties
known as Yädava, Mädhava and Våñëi had their origin from Yadu,
Madhu and Våñëi.

text: O Mahäräja Parékñit, because Yadu, Madhu and
sanskrit:
Våñëi each inaugurated a dynasty, their dynasties are known as
Yädava, Mädhava and Våñëi. The son of Yadu named Kroñöä had a
son named Våjinavän. The son of Våjinavän was Svähita; the son of
Svähita, Viñadgu; the son of Viñadgu, Citraratha; and the son of
Citraratha, Çaçabindu. The greatly fortunate Çaçabindu, who was a
great mystic, possessed fourteen opulences and was the owner of fourteen
great jewels. Thus he became the emperor of the world.

text: The famous Çaçabindu had ten thousand wives, and by each
sanskrit:
he begot a lakh of sons. Therefore the number of his sons was ten
thousand lakhs.

text: Among these many sons, six were the foremost, such as
sanskrit:
Påthuçravä and Påthukérti. The son of Påthuçravä was known as
Dharma, and his son was known as Uçanä. Uçanä was the performer of
one hundred horse sacrifices.

text: The son of Uçanä was Rucaka, who had five sons-Purujit,
sanskrit:
Rukma, Rukmeñu, Påthu and Jyämagha. Please hear of these sons from
me.

text: Jyämagha had no sons, but because he was fearful of his
sanskrit:
wife, Çaibyä, he could not accept another wife. Jyämagha once took
from the house of some royal enemy a girl who was a prostitute, but upon
seeing her Çaibyä was very angry and said to her husband, "My husband,
you cheater, who is this girl sitting upon my seat on the chariot?"
Jyämagha then replied, "This girl will be your daughter-in-law." Upon
hearing these joking words, Çaibyä smilingly replied.

text: Çaibyä said, "I am sterile and have no co-wife. How can
sanskrit:
this girl be my daughter-in-law? Please tell me." Jyämagha replied, "My
dear Queen, I shall see that you indeed have a son and that this girl
will be your daughter-in-law."

text: Long, long ago, Jyämagha had satisfied the demigods and
sanskrit:
Pitäs by worshiping them. Now, by their mercy, Jyämagha's words came
true. Although Çaibyä was barren, by the grace of the demigods she
became pregnant and in due course of time gave birth to a child named
Vidarbha. Before the child's birth, the girl had been accepted as a
daughter-in-law, and therefore Vidarbha actually married her when he
grew up.
